note: Lesson sheets of the draft curriculum, generated by scripts/build_curriculum.py from docs/curriculum/weeks/. The application shows a day's sheet only when the day's objective texts equal the ones recorded here, so a sheet is never shown against a curriculum it was not written for. Content of a PROPOSED curriculum: reading, not a record.

1.title: Linux, Python and secure lab engineering
1.purpose: Build the laboratory the next eleven weeks depend on and show, with evidence, that it is authorized, isolated and reproducible. Then make the two working tools of the program usable: the Linux command line (files, permissions, processes, logs) and Python for handling security data safely. Everything later is judged by the habits set here: state the scope, record the baseline, change one thing at a time, keep the evidence.
1.lab_stack: One Linux workstation with a hypervisor (KVM/QEMU with libvirt, or VirtualBox), 16 GB RAM or more (32 GB is needed from week 6), 250 GB of free SSD, Python 3.11 or newer with `venv`, and git. Guests attach only to an isolated virtual network. Evidence lives in `~/g9lab/evidence/`, owned by you, mode 0700, never inside a guest. Synthetic data only: no real credentials, no real personal data, no network targets that are not yours.
1.accelerator: An experienced administrator can take the Day 1 diagnostic first and treat days 2 and 3 as review; the Saturday assessment still happens, unchanged.

2.title: Networking, protocols and scoped reconnaissance
2.purpose: Read the network as evidence. By Friday you can say, from a capture and from the hosts themselves, which layer a failure lives in, why a packet took the path it did, what a DNS answer is really saying, which flows a policy allows and which it blocks, and how much a scan result can be trusted. Reconnaissance is taught last and only inside a written scope, because it is the week's authorization lesson: the tool is easy, the permission is the skill.
2.lab_stack: The week 1 lab plus two guests: `lin-aux` (client) and `net-router` (Linux with forwarding and nftables), on two isolated subnets, and a capture point on every link (`tcpdump`, Wireshark or `tshark`). Python 3 with the `ipaddress` module. Optional: scapy for building packets. Snapshot every guest before each lab.
2.accelerator: A network engineer can skip the subnetting and routing drills of days 7 and 10 after getting them all right from memory in the Monday recall block, and spend the time on the independent labs; days 8, 9 and 11 and the Saturday assessment stay.

3.title: Web application fundamentals
3.purpose: Understand how a web application decides who you are and what you may do, and how that decision fails. You build a small application of your own, find its defects the way a tester would, fix them the way an engineer would, and prove each fix with a test that failed before it. The same four ideas carry through the week: the browser is a hostile environment for secrets, identity is state, every object needs its own authorization check, and data must never be allowed to become code.
3.lab_stack: The week 1 lab plus a web guest. A small Python web application of your own (Flask or FastAPI with SQLite), written by you on day 13 and kept in git with one branch per planted defect; a browser with developer tools; `curl`; `mitmproxy` or another intercepting proxy; `pytest`. For independent practice a free account on the PortSwigger Web Security Academy and the OWASP Juice Shop run locally in a container. All of it stays on the isolated lab network, with synthetic data.
3.accelerator: An application security engineer can build the lab application in half the time and spend the saved time on the independent labs; the Saturday assessment is taken unchanged.

4.title: Advanced web and API security
4.purpose: Move from single-page defects to the failures that live in how a system is put together: identity carried by tokens across services, servers that fetch what users tell them to fetch, files and objects that arrive from outside, business rules that only hold when requests arrive one at a time, and the habit of writing down what could go wrong before it does. The week ends with a threat model of your own application, built from evidence you collected, and with the blind API assessment.
4.lab_stack: The week 3 lab. A small REST API of your own (FastAPI with a JWT library and SQLite) with two tenants and three roles; an internal-only service on a second subnet that plays the part of an administrative or metadata endpoint; the lab DNS server of week 2; `pytest` and `httpx`; the OWASP crAPI running locally from its containers for independent practice. All traffic stays on the isolated lab network, with synthetic data.
4.accelerator: A penetration tester can build the API in half the time and use the saved hours on the independent labs; the threat model of day 23 and the Saturday assessment are taken unchanged.

5.title: Host security and privilege boundaries
5.purpose: A host is a set of principals and the rules that say what each can make the machine do. This week you learn to read those rules on Windows and on Linux, find the places where a low-privilege principal can become a higher one, record what a defender would see when that happens, and write down a hardened state that you can test by behaviour rather than by reading configuration. The Saturday assessment gives you a host you have not seen and asks for the same four things: diagnose, explain, repair, prove.
5.lab_stack: The week 1 Linux guests plus a Windows guest from a Microsoft evaluation image (verify the terms and the evaluation period when you download it; it must outlast the program), on the isolated network. Windows: PowerShell, the Sysinternals tools (Process Explorer, Autoruns, AccessChk, Sysmon) and event viewing with `Get-WinEvent`. Linux: `sudo`, `getcap`, `auditd`, `systemd-analyze`, Lynis or OpenSCAP. Every weakness in the week is one you plant yourself in a snapshot-restorable guest, with harmless markers instead of payloads.
5.accelerator: A systems administrator who can list a host's service accounts, capabilities and autostart locations from memory in the Monday recall block can treat days 25 and 28 as review; days 26, 27 and 29 and the Saturday assessment stay.

6.title: Active Directory and identity
6.purpose: In most organisations identity is the control plane: whoever can act as a privileged principal can act as the organisation. This week you build a small Active Directory forest, learn to read it as a graph of trust and permission rather than as a directory of names, understand Kerberos well enough to diagnose it when it fails, find the delegation and permission paths that lead to privileged groups, close them, and write the detections that would show someone using them. The privileged group in your lab is a surrogate, so nothing you demonstrate can damage the domain.
6.lab_stack: The week 5 lab plus a domain: one domain controller, one member server and one client from Microsoft evaluation images (verify the terms and the evaluation period at download), forest `corp.lab.test` on the isolated network, 16 GB of RAM for the three guests at the least. Tools: the PowerShell Active Directory module, `dsacls`, `setspn`, `nltest`, `klist`, Wireshark's Kerberos dissector, BloodHound Community Edition for graph analysis of your own lab, and `Get-WinEvent`. A lighter fallback is a Samba domain controller on Linux; it differs from Windows in places you must note. The Game of Active Directory lab is an optional extra for week 12.
6.accelerator: An identity engineer who can draw the Kerberos exchange with the ticket contents from memory in the Tuesday recall block can treat day 32 as review; days 33 to 35 and the Saturday assessment stay.

7.title: SOC, detection and threat hunting
7.purpose: Detection is engineering: a pipeline that collects the right events, makes them comparable, expresses a hypothesis about abuse as a rule, tests the rule against what must and must not match, and measures what it costs in false alarms. This week you build that pipeline over the lab you have been attacking and defending for six weeks, write portable rules for the behaviours you have already seen, and learn to reconstruct what happened from several sources while keeping facts apart from inference. The Saturday assessment gives you telemetry you have not seen and asks for an investigation and two tested detections.
7.lab_stack: The week 6 lab plus a log pipeline: a collector guest, a forwarder on each Linux and Windows guest (Fluent Bit, Vector or an equivalent), network sensor logs from Zeek or Suricata on the router, and a store you can query (files with Python and SQLite are enough; OpenSearch is optional). Sigma tooling: pySigma with the backend for the store you chose. Public datasets of your choice, with their licences checked. Synthetic data and your own lab's activity only; no real logs of any organisation.
7.accelerator: A detection engineer who already writes tested Sigma rules can build the pipeline from existing tooling on day 37 and spend the time on the independent labs; days 39 to 41's fixtures and the Saturday assessment stay.

8.title: DFIR, malware and hunting
8.purpose: When detection fires, someone has to decide what happened, how bad it is and what to do, using evidence that can be trusted. This week covers the whole path on lab systems: scoping and severity, preserving evidence so that it survives scrutiny, reading host artifacts and network captures, building a timeline in which every statement is labelled, triaging a suspicious program by static means only, and hunting through telemetry for what no rule has found. The Saturday assessment gives you an incident dataset you have not seen and asks for triage, a timeline and a recovery recommendation.
8.lab_stack: The week 7 lab plus acquisition and analysis tools: disk and memory images taken from lab guests (the hypervisor can dump a guest's memory and copy its disk image), the Sleuth Kit or Autopsy, Plaso, Volatility 3, Zeek and Wireshark, YARA, `capa`, Python with `pefile`, and your own benign fixtures. Malware work is **static only**, on fixtures you compile yourself or that a training source provides as safe. Do not execute an unknown program. A real sample is handled only in a disposable guest with no network and a snapshot, after you have decided in writing to do so.
8.accelerator: An incident responder who can state the order of volatility and the custody record fields from memory in the Monday recall block can treat the acquisition half of day 43 as review; days 44 to 47 and the Saturday assessment stay.

9.title: LLM application and RAG security
9.purpose: A language model is a component that turns text into text and cannot tell instructions from data. An application built around one inherits that property: whatever reaches the model, from the user, a document, a web page or a tool, can try to steer it. This week you build a small retrieval-augmented application of your own, map its trust boundaries, attack it with harmless goals, and learn which defences are guarantees (deterministic code outside the model) and which are statistics (behaviour of the model, measured with intervals). The rule that runs through the week is the one this program's own application follows: model output is data, never an instruction and never authoritative, and authority is decided in code.
9.lab_stack: The week 8 lab plus an application guest with no network access except to a local model server. A local model runtime (llama.cpp's server or Ollama) with a small open-weight instruction model whose licence permits your use (record the name, version, file hash and quantisation), a local embedding model, a vector store you can inspect (SQLite-based or a Python library), and a small web or command-line front end of your own. Evaluation tools: `pytest`, `promptfoo`, `garak` or an equivalent scanner. A synthetic corpus of company-style documents for three tenants and three roles, with canary strings (unique, meaningless tokens) planted in restricted documents. No real data, no network egress, and no attempt to make the model produce harmful content: every adversarial goal in the week is harmless (reveal a canary, call a tool with a marker).
9.accelerator: An engineer who has built retrieval applications can write the lab application in half the time and spend the saved hours on the independent labs; the evaluation design of day 53 and the Saturday assessment are taken unchanged.

10.title: Agent security, MCP and tool authorization
10.purpose: An agent is a language model in a loop with tools: it decides, calls, reads the result and decides again. Every tool is a grant of authority, every tool result is a new input to the model, and every step is a chance for text to change what happens next. This week you build a small agent of your own and take apart its authority: where authority crosses a boundary, whose identity each call carries, what a protocol such as the Model Context Protocol adds and what it leaves to you, what persistent memory does to trust, and how to test defences in a bounded experiment that you design before you see the result. The rule from week 9 gets stricter: the model proposes, code disposes, and the code that disposes holds the authority.
10.lab_stack: The week 9 lab plus an agent loop of your own (a few hundred lines of Python), a sandbox container for tools with no network by default and a mounted scratch directory, a local authorization server for tokens (a small OAuth-style service you write or a lightweight open-source one), an MCP server and client written with an official software development kit, a memory store you can inspect, and a scripted adversarial model stub from week 9. Pin the specification revision of the protocol you test against and read its change log; the protocol is changing quickly and the authorization rules in particular have been revised several times. Synthetic data only; every adversarial goal is harmless.
10.accelerator: An engineer who has shipped agent features can build the lab agent in half the time and spend the saved hours on the independent labs and the pre-registered experiment of day 59; the Saturday assessment is taken unchanged.

11.title: AI red-team, evaluation and supply chain
11.purpose: The last two weeks secured one application and one agent. This week widens the view to the AI system as a whole: its assets (data, models, indexes, prompts, tools, pipelines), the threats against each across the life cycle (collection, training, packaging, serving, use), how to test those threats honestly, where a model or a dependency comes from and whether you should trust it, what training and evaluation data can leak, and how to design measures that mean what they claim. A red team here is a bounded, pre-registered, harmless experiment, not a performance. The Saturday assessment hands you an unfamiliar AI system and asks for a threat model, bounded tests and findings across all of it.
11.lab_stack: The week 10 lab plus a small machine-learning workbench: Python with scikit-learn and a small synthetic text or tabular dataset for classical models, a model registry directory of your own with hashes and licences, a package index mirror or a hash-pinned requirements file, and `picklescan` or an equivalent. Everything stays on the isolated network. Adversarial work targets your own models and applications with harmless goals; no harmful content is generated, collected or stored.
11.accelerator: A machine-learning engineer who can name the assets and life-cycle stages of an AI system and the attacks of each from memory in the Monday recall block can treat day 61 as review; days 62 to 65 and the Saturday assessment stay.

12.title: Integrated G9/CT9 capstone
12.purpose: Eleven weeks of separate skills now have to work together on one system the way a real engagement works: a written scope, a threat model across layers, an assessment that follows an access chain from the outside to something that matters, detection and response reasoning, an assessment of the AI components, and a report that defends every claim with evidence. The week is a rehearsal of an engagement from authorization to report, ending with a blind integrated practical and the portfolio that records what you can do and what you cannot yet.
12.lab_stack: Everything from weeks 1 to 11, joined into one integrated environment, "the estate": two network zones behind a router, the web application and API of weeks 3 and 4, a Linux host and a Windows domain of weeks 5 and 6, the log pipeline of week 7, and the assistant, agent and one MCP server of weeks 9 and 10, with a canary document standing in for the crown jewel. A second person, or a script you have not read, plants faults across the layers and a benign incident in the telemetry, and seals the list. Isolation, authorization, synthetic data and harmless goals apply exactly as before. The evidence of the capstone is kept in one repository with an index and hashes.
12.competencies: All eight packs: this week revisits `lab.authorization`, `recon.scope-definition`, `web.threat-model-logic`, `ai.threat-model-redteam`, `net.failure-diagnosis`, `web.authz-idor`, `api.token-authz`, `linux.privilege-boundaries`, `ad.delegation-permissions`, `ad.kerberos`, `det.sigma-rules`, `dfir.host-artifacts`, `ir.recovery-recommendation`, `agent.workflow-authority`, `mcp.transport-auth`, `llm.prompt-injection` and others, each in the setting where it matters most: together.
12.accelerator: None: the capstone is the accelerator's end point. An experienced practitioner takes it unchanged and is graded on the same rubric.

D01.title: Lab authorization and boundaries
objectives: Define lab authorization and boundaries — write a one-page scope statement: owner, permitted systems and actions, forbidden targets, data rules, time window and stop condition

Map host/guest and evidence isolation — draw the host, guest, network and evidence-store boundaries and prove with commands that a guest cannot reach the internet, the host's services or the evidence store
Establish diagnostic baseline — record the clean state of the lab (snapshot ids, listening ports, running services, hashes of key files) and score yourself on the week's diagnostic

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Nothing to recall yet, so take the entry check instead. Without notes, write one line each: What is the difference between authorization and scope? What makes a lab isolated rather than merely separate? Name three facts you would record to prove that a system returned to a known state.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Authorization is permission from someone entitled to give it, for named systems, actions and times. Scope is the boundary of that permission. A lab is authorized because it is yours and stays inside what you wrote down; an engagement against anyone else's systems needs their written permission first.
- Isolation is demonstrated, not declared. List the trust zones (host, guests, evidence store), then the flows that are allowed between them. Every other flow must fail, and you show that it fails.
- A baseline is a recorded, reproducible known-good state. Without it you cannot tell drift from damage, and you cannot prove a restore worked.
- Read the planning and rules-of-engagement guidance in NIST SP 800-115 and note the elements a rules-of-engagement document names.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Create `~/g9lab/{vms,images,evidence,work,scripts}`; make `evidence` mode 0700. Record `uname -a`, `lsblk`, `ip -br address` into `evidence/host-0.txt` and its `sha256sum`.
2. Install the hypervisor. Define an isolated virtual network with no forwarding (in libvirt, a network definition without a `forward` element) and no DHCP uplink.
3. Create one minimal Linux guest named `lin-target`, attach it only to that network, and take a snapshot named `clean-0`.
4. Prove isolation from the guest: no default route to the internet (a request to a public address fails within three seconds), no access to host services other than the ones you list, no mount of the evidence directory. Record each command and its observed output.
5. Capture the baseline inside the guest: listening sockets (`ss -tulpn`), running units (`systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running`), installed package list, and `sha256sum` of `/etc` and of the binaries in `/usr/bin`. Store the files in `evidence/` and hash them from the host.
6. Take the diagnostic: for each of the eight competencies of the week, do one small task from memory and score it 0 (could not), 1 (with documentation), 2 (from memory). Keep the scores.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Without opening your guided-lab notes, build a second guest `lin-aux` and bring it to the same state: same isolation, same baseline capture. Then compare the two baselines and explain every difference as intended, drift or error. Finally write the rules of engagement for a pretend assessment of a web application you will build in week 3: three things in scope, three out of scope, who can stop it, how evidence is handled.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a drift check (shell or Python) that recomputes the baseline of a guest and reports added, removed and changed items. Make three deliberate changes (a new listening port, an edited configuration file, a new user) and confirm that all three are reported and that an untouched guest reports nothing. Then restore `clean-0` and confirm the check is silent.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Assemble the hand-in as a short report with these parts: the scope statement (one page, dated, signed by you as owner); the boundary diagram with allowed flows labelled; the isolation proof with commands, outputs and timestamps; the baseline files with their SHA-256 values; the diagnostic scores; and a list of what the baseline cannot show. It is accepted when a stranger could rebuild the lab and reach the same baseline from the report alone.

D01.watch_for: Calling a network "isolated" because it has no gateway configured on the guest: check the host's side too. Keeping evidence inside the machine you are testing. A baseline taken after you already changed something.
D01.resources:
- `https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/115/final`: SP 800-115 (September 2008). NIST publication, freely available
- `https://libvirt.org/formatnetwork.html`: current documentation; pin the libvirt version you install. open documentation, ASSUMED
- `https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/`: current man-pages project; pin the release you read. freely readable, ASSUMED

D02.title: Filesystem, permissions and ownership
objectives: Explain filesystem hierarchy — place 15 given paths into their purpose in the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard and justify each placement without notes
Demonstrate permission/ownership controls — configure owner, group, mode bits, the setgid and sticky bits and one POSIX ACL so that a stated access matrix holds, and verify every cell with test users

Diagnose controlled access failure — from a "permission denied" report, find the failing path component and its exact cause (mode, owner, ACL, mount option or security module) and fix it with the smallest change

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the five elements of a scope statement. Why does the baseline not prove the system is secure? Which command showed you the guest had no route out, and what did it print?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The hierarchy has purposes, not folders: `/etc` host configuration, `/var` variable state and logs, `/usr` installed software, `/run` runtime state, `/proc` and `/sys` kernel views, `/dev` devices, `/tmp` shared scratch space.
- Access is decided per path component: the kernel needs execute (search) permission on every directory on the way, then the right bit on the file. Read `path_resolution(7)` and `credentials(7)`.
- Mode bits apply to owner, group and others; setuid and setgid change the effective identity of an executable, setgid on a directory passes the group to new files, the sticky bit stops deleting files you do not own. An ACL adds named users and groups, limited by its mask.
- Permissions can also be refused by a mount option (`ro`, `noexec`, `nosuid`, `nodev`) or by a security module such as AppArmor or SELinux even when the mode bits allow the access.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Restore `clean-0`. Create users `alice`, `bob`, `carol` and a group `analysts` with `alice` and `bob`.
2. Build `/srv/case/{intake,work,reports}`. Write the target matrix first (a table of path by user with r, w, x): `intake` writable by analysts but files deletable only by their owners; `work` shared by the group with new files inheriting the group; `reports` readable by `carol` and not writable by her.
3. Implement it with `chown`, `chmod` (including setgid and the sticky bit), `setfacl` for `carol`, and verify each cell with `sudo -u USER test -r|-w|-x PATH` and `namei -l PATH`.
4. Fill the matrix with the observed result next to the intended one. Any difference is a finding.
5. Break one cell on purpose (remove execute on a parent directory) and write down the exact sequence you followed to find it.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three different access failures in a fresh clone of the guest (a directory without search permission, a script on a `noexec` mount, an ACL mask that hides a grant). Draw one at random without looking at the others, and diagnose it from the symptom and your method alone. Repeat with a second one. Record time to diagnosis and which instrument found the cause.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a permission audit that lists, for a given tree, every world-writable file or directory without the sticky bit, every setuid or setgid file, and every file owned by no existing user. Run it on `/srv/case` and on the guest's `/usr` and `/etc`, explain each finding as expected or a problem, and confirm the audit reports your planted problem.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the worksheet: matrix (intended and observed), commands, the diagnosis log of the deliberate failure, and the audit output with your reading of each finding. It is accepted when every matrix cell has an observed result and each difference is explained.

D02.watch_for: Testing as root, which passes everything. Forgetting the ACL mask. Fixing a failure by `chmod 777`: the smallest change that satisfies the matrix is the answer.
D02.resources:
- `https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/fhs.shtml`: FHS 3.0. published standard, freely readable, ASSUMED
- `https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/path_resolution.7.html`: current man-pages project. freely readable, ASSUMED
- `https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man5/acl.5.html`: current man-pages project. freely readable, ASSUMED

D03.title: Processes, services and logging
objectives: Analyze processes/services — map one running service from unit file to process tree, open files, sockets, cgroup and user, and explain what restricts it
Inspect system logging — locate where an event is recorded (journal, authentication log, audit), query it by unit, time and priority, and state what the logs cannot tell you
Reproduce troubleshooting workflow — break and repair a service in a documented sequence of hypothesis, test, observation, change and check that another person can replay

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what does the sticky bit do on a directory? What reads the ACL mask? Draw the access path from `alice` to `/srv/case/reports/x.txt` and name every permission checked.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A service is a unit definition, a process (or tree) in a control group, an identity, a set of open files and sockets, and restrictions (sandboxing options, capabilities, resource limits).
- Logs are produced by different writers with different trust: the journal collects what services write to standard streams and the system logger; authentication events come from PAM and the SSH daemon; the audit subsystem records kernel-observed events by rule. Logs can be missing, rotated, clock-skewed or written by the thing you are investigating.
- A troubleshooting method beats intuition: state the symptom, form competing hypotheses, choose the test that separates them, change one thing, observe, check the symptom, write it down.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. In `lin-target` install a small network service of your choice (for example a web server) and enable it.
2. Map it: `systemctl status`, `systemctl cat`, `ps -eo pid,ppid,user,cgroup,cmd --forest`, `ss -tulpn`, `ls -l /proc/PID/fd`, and the unit's sandboxing options from `systemd-analyze security UNIT`.
3. Find its events three ways: `journalctl -u UNIT --since`, the service's own log file, and an audit rule watching its configuration file. Trigger one event and find it in each place; note the differences in detail and timing.
4. Break the service three ways (wrong ownership of its configuration, a port already in use, a missing dependency). For each, write the symptom, the competing hypotheses, the test that separated them and the repair.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: In a fresh clone, install a different service you have not used and prepare two faults for it. Draw one at random and diagnose it using only the method and the logs, writing the log as you go in the format of the guided lab. Then give your log to a clean clone and replay it step by step: it must reproduce the fault and the repair.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Harden the service from step 2: restrict it with unit sandboxing options so that `systemd-analyze security` improves, then prove the service still works and that a deliberately forbidden action (writing outside its state directory) now fails. Write the one-line rationale for each option you added.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the diagnostic report: service map, the three places the event appeared with a comparison, the three repair logs, and the hardening diff with its proof. It is accepted when the repair logs can be replayed by someone else and the report states at least two things the logs could not show.

D03.watch_for: Reading a log you cannot date. Changing two things at once. Confusing "the service started" with "the service works".
D03.resources:
- `https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/`: current systemd manual pages; pin the systemd version of your guest. open documentation, ASSUMED
- `https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/cgroups.7.html`: current man-pages project. freely readable, ASSUMED

D04.title: Parsing security records in Python
objectives: Parse structured security records in Python — write a parser for one log format (authentication log lines or JSON lines) that yields typed records with validated fields
Handle malformed inputs safely — define and test the behaviour for truncated, oversized, mis-encoded, duplicated and hostile lines without a crash, unbounded memory use or a silent drop
Test parser with fixtures — build a fixture suite (valid, boundary, malformed) that fails when the parser is deliberately broken

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which three places record that a service started? Name two things a log cannot prove. State your troubleshooting method in six words, and write the one command that lists the sockets a service holds open.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Parsing is a security boundary: input is hostile until it has been parsed into a type with limits. Decide the contract first: accepted forms, maximum sizes, character encoding, what happens to a rejected line (counted, quarantined, reported).
- Safe by default means small, explicit and testable: dataclasses or typed dictionaries, explicit `datetime` handling in UTC, no `eval`, no unbounded regular expressions on untrusted input, streaming rather than reading whole files.
- Tests are the specification. A fixture suite should be able to say "this input must be rejected" as clearly as "this one must be accepted".

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Create a repository with `src/`, `tests/` and `fixtures/`; use a virtual environment and a pinned `requirements.txt`.
2. Write a streaming parser for one format. Required fields, types and ranges are written down first. Timestamps become timezone-aware UTC values.
3. Add a rejection path: each rejected line is counted by reason and kept (bounded) for review.
4. Add tests for ten valid lines and ten malformed ones. Run them.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Extend the parser to a second format without changing the first one's behaviour. Write a hostile fixture set: a 50 MB line, a line with invalid UTF-8, a line with embedded control characters that could forge a log entry, a duplicated record, a timestamp in the future, a field with a surprising type. State beforehand what the parser must do for each, then run them. Measure peak memory on the 50 MB line.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Break the parser on purpose in four ways (accept a type it should refuse, drop the size limit, swallow an exception, mishandle timezones) and confirm the suite fails each time. Add a test that proves each defence by failing without it. Record which of your four breakages the original suite did not catch.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the repository state (commit id), the test output, and a one-page review: contract, rejected-input table, memory measurement, and the breakages the suite missed with the tests you added. It is accepted when the suite fails for every deliberate breakage.

D04.watch_for: Parsing with a regular expression that backtracks on a long line. Local time with no zone. A test that passes because the fixture never reaches the code under test.

D05.title: Version control, runbooks and evidence completeness
objectives: Apply version-control concepts — keep the lab files, parser and notes in git with meaningful commits, develop a change on a branch and revert a bad change

Produce reproducible runbook — write a runbook that a peer can follow to rebuild the day-3 failure and repair on a fresh guest with identical results, ending with checks that verify the guest matches the recorded baseline
Assess evidence completeness — review your own week's evidence against a checklist of who, what, when, where, how, hash and limits, and list the gaps and what would close them

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what makes a parser's rejection path testable? Name two inputs that were dangerous in your own fixtures. What does the drift check from day 1 not detect?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Version control records why as well as what: small commits, messages that state intent, branches for experiments, tags for states you will refer to. A secret committed once is committed forever; keep secrets out and rotate any that leak.
- A runbook is executable documentation: prerequisites, exact commands, expected output at each step, a stop condition, and a rollback. If a step needs judgement, say what the judgement is based on.
- Evidence is complete when a reader can answer: who produced it, what it shows, when, from where, by what method, with what integrity check, and what it does not show.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Put `~/g9lab/scripts`, the parser repository and your runbooks under git (the evidence directory is not committed; its hashes are).
2. Make a change on a branch, commit it in two steps, merge it, then introduce a defect, find the commit with `git bisect` or `git log -S`, and revert it.
3. Write the runbook for the day-3 failure of your choice, with expected output beside each command and a last section that verifies the guest against the day 1 baseline.
4. Execute your runbook on a fresh clone of `clean-0` exactly as written. Every step that did not work as written is a defect in the runbook: fix it and run again until the run is clean.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Give your runbook to a second environment: a clean clone, with a different user and no memory of your earlier session (restart the guest, discard your shell history). Follow it again as if you had not written it, and keep a list of every place you relied on something that was not written down. Then do the same for the drift check of day 1.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Add a pre-commit check that refuses a commit containing common secret patterns (private key headers, long random-looking tokens, passwords in configuration) and prove it blocks a planted fake secret and allows a normal change. State what it cannot catch.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the runbook, the git history excerpt that shows the branch, the bad change and its revert, and the completeness review: a table of every piece of evidence from days 1 to 4 with the seven questions answered, the gaps, and the action to close each. It is accepted when the runbook succeeded on a fresh guest and every gap has an action.

D05.watch_for: A runbook written from memory after the fact. Evidence without a hash or a time. Secrets in history.

D07.title: Layers, addressing and pathways
objectives: Map OSI/TCP-IP layers — for one exchange between two lab guests name each layer's unit of data, address and protocol, and capture one packet that shows the headers of every layer
Explain addressing and subnetting — given a prefix compute network, broadcast, mask, usable range and host count by hand, verify with a tool, and say why two hosts are or are not on-link
Diagram network pathways — draw the path of a packet to a neighbour and across the router, with each hop's address rewriting and the next-hop resolution, and check the diagram against captures

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which seven questions does the evidence completeness checklist ask of every piece of evidence? State your troubleshooting method in six words. What does `ss -tulpn` show that `systemctl status` does not?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Encapsulation: an application message becomes a TCP or UDP segment, then an IP packet, then an Ethernet frame. Each layer adds a header that the layer below treats as data. The OSI model is a teaching vocabulary; the Internet protocol suite is what runs.
- An IPv4 prefix splits an address into network and host bits. Two hosts are on-link when their addresses share the sender's prefix; otherwise the sender uses its default gateway. On a link the next hop is found by ARP (IPv6: neighbour discovery) and the frame is rewritten at every router while the IP addresses stay end to end, unless something translates them.
- Private ranges (RFC 1918), link-local addresses and loopback are not routed on the Internet. A /30 has two usable hosts, a /31 is a point-to-point link, a /24 has 254 usable hosts.
- Read RFC 791 and the first sections of RFC 9293, then the Wireshark guide's chapter on capturing.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write the addressing plan before touching a guest: subnet A `10.20.1.0/24` (`lin-target`, `lin-aux`), subnet B `10.20.2.0/24` (a third guest), `net-router` with one address in each.
2. Create the two isolated virtual networks, attach the guests, set addresses with `ip address add`, routes with `ip route add`, enable forwarding on the router (`sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward=1`). Check with `ip -br address` and `ip route get ADDRESS` on every guest.
3. Capture on both router interfaces while a guest in A fetches a page from the guest in B. For one packet write down: Ethernet source and destination, IP source and destination, TTL, TCP ports, payload. Do it on both interfaces and show that MAC addresses changed, IP addresses did not, and the TTL fell by one.
4. By hand, then with `python3 -c "import ipaddress; ..."`: network, broadcast, usable range and host count of `192.168.10.77/27`, `172.16.5.130/25` and `10.0.0.9/30`.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Design an addressing plan for a pretend office with 60 users, 25 servers and 10 management devices using the smallest prefix that fits each, with room to grow by half. Implement it across the guests, make users able to reach servers and not management using routes only (no firewall yet), prove each with `ip route get` and a capture, then draw the pathway diagram from memory and correct it against the captures.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Duplicate addresses and neighbour-table tampering break the assumption that an address names one machine. Write a small script that reads `ip neigh` (or a capture) and alerts when one IP address is claimed by a second hardware address. Plant a conflict in the lab (give two guests the same address) and detect it with your script and with `arping -D`; then show the script is silent on the clean network and state one way an attacker on the link could avoid your alert.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the map: addressing plan (table), the subnet arithmetic, the annotated captures with file names and SHA-256 values, the path diagram, and a list of every place the diagram and the capture disagreed and how you resolved it. It is accepted when each claim on the diagram points to a capture.

D07.watch_for: Reading the capture on the wrong interface. Forgetting that a router's two sides see different frames. Treating the TTL as a distance rather than a counter.

D08.title: TCP states and failure interpretation
objectives: Explain TCP states — from a capture label the handshake, data transfer, teardown and reset, and name the state of each endpoint at every point

Interpret retransmission/failure PCAP — identify retransmissions, duplicate acknowledgements, a zero window, resets and half-open connections in a capture and say what each indicates about the path or the endpoint

Diagnose connectivity in lab — given reports that a service is unreachable, separate an unreachable host, a closed port, a filtered port, a listener on the wrong interface and an application fault using `ss`, a capture and one probe

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: draw the three guest-to-guest hops of yesterday's path. Which field changes at every router and which does not? Compute the usable host range of `10.20.4.0/26`.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The states are LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1 and -2, CLOSE-WAIT, LAST-ACK, CLOSING and TIME-WAIT. Sequence and acknowledgement numbers count bytes; the window limits what is in flight.
- What a refusal looks like depends on who answers: a closed port answers a SYN with a reset; a firewall that drops answers nothing, so the sender retransmits its SYN with growing delay and then gives up; a firewall that rejects answers with a reset or an ICMP error.
- Loss shows as retransmissions after a timeout, or as a fast retransmit after three duplicate acknowledgements; a zero window means the receiver's buffer is full, which is the application's problem, not the network's.
- Read the TCP sections of RFC 9293 on the state diagram and on retransmission.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Run a listener on `lin-target` (`python3 -m http.server 8080`). Capture a full request from `lin-aux`, with display filter `tcp.port == 8080`. Label every packet with the state of both ends.
2. Make the port closed (stop the listener) and capture the refusal. Then make it filtered with an nftables rule that drops, and again with one that rejects; capture each and note the difference in what the client sees and how long it takes.
3. Bind the listener to `127.0.0.1` only and show from `lin-aux` what that looks like, and how `ss -tln` on the target shows the cause.
4. Add loss and delay on the target's interface (`tc qdisc add dev IF root netem loss 5% delay 80ms`) and capture a transfer. Find the retransmissions with `tcp.analysis.retransmission` and a duplicate-acknowledgement sequence.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three faults of different kinds on three clones (a service bound to the wrong interface, a drop rule on one port, a listener that accepts and never replies). Draw one at random and diagnose it from the symptom ("the page does not load") using at most a client, `ss` and one capture. Write the order in which you ruled hypotheses out. Repeat with a second fault and compare which instrument settled each.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Rate-limit new connections to the service with an nftables rule (for example `ct state new limit rate 20/second accept`, then drop the rest) and prove two things: a burst from `lin-aux` hits the limit (the counter moves, some connections fail) and an ordinary client below the limit is unaffected. State what the rule does not protect against.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in three annotated captures with the endpoint state at each step, the table of failure signatures (closed, dropped, rejected, loopback-only, lossy, application stalled) with the observation that identifies each, and the diagnosis logs of the independent lab. It is accepted when each failure signature is shown in a capture of your own.

D08.watch_for: Concluding "the firewall blocks it" from silence alone: silence also means loss or a dead host. Comparing a client-side and a server-side capture without allowing for clock difference.

D09.title: DNS resolution, caching and failure
objectives: Trace recursive/authoritative DNS — follow a resolution from the stub resolver through the recursive resolver to the authoritative server and explain each referral, record type and TTL
Analyze resolution cache and failure — show how TTLs and negative caching change answers over time and read the fields of the DNS messages in a capture (identifier, flags, response code, sections)
Diagnose test DNS defect — find a planted fault (missing record, wrong glue, lame delegation, a TTL that is too long, a resolver pointing at the wrong server) from the symptom to the cause

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what does a closed port, a dropped port and a rejected port each look like to the client? What does `ss -tln` show for a service bound to `127.0.0.1`? Name two TCP states that persist after a connection ends.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The stub resolver on a host asks a recursive resolver, which walks the hierarchy (root, top-level domain, the zone's authoritative servers), caches what it learns for each record's TTL, and caches failures for a shorter time (negative caching).
- A referral is not an answer: it points to the next servers. Glue records give addresses for name servers inside the zone they serve. A delegation that points at a server that does not answer for the zone is lame.
- Message fields to read: query identifier, flags (QR, AA, RD, RA, TC), response code (NOERROR, NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, REFUSED) and the answer, authority and additional sections. `.test` is reserved for testing and never exists in the public DNS.
- Read RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 on resolution, and RFC 2308 on negative caching.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. On one guest run an authoritative server for the zone `lab.test` (BIND or NSD) and on another a recursive resolver (Unbound) configured to ask it for that zone. Point a client at the recursive resolver.
2. Walk the resolution by hand with `dig +norecurse` against each server, noting flags, TTL and sections. Capture the whole exchange and annotate it.
3. Resolve the same name twice, a few seconds apart, and show the TTL falling in the cached answer. Query a name that does not exist twice and show the negative answer's lifetime.
4. Change a record on the authoritative server without changing its serial, then with a new serial, and describe what the recursive resolver and a fresh client see over the next minutes.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three faults (a delegation to a server that is down, a missing glue record, a client configured with a resolver that has no route). Draw one at random and find it using `dig`, a capture and the server logs only. Record the sequence of tests. Then explain in writing why the same user-visible symptom, "the name does not resolve", has at least four distinct causes and which test separates them.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Restrict the guests so that only the internal recursive resolver may send DNS traffic (drop outbound port 53 from every other source) and turn on query logging on the resolver. Write a script that flags names with unusually long labels or unusually many distinct subdomains of one parent in a window. Test it with synthetic names that mimic a tunnel and with normal traffic, record false positives, and state what a patient adversary can do to stay under your thresholds.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the DNS investigation: the traced resolution with message fields, the TTL evidence, the diagnosis log of the fault you drew and a table of "does not resolve" causes with the test that identifies each. It is accepted when every claim names a capture or log line.

D09.watch_for: Forgetting that the client's own cache and the resolver's cache both exist. Editing a zone and not raising its serial. Testing against the wrong server because `/etc/resolv.conf` was rewritten.

D10.title: Routing, NAT and segmentation
objectives: Explain route selection — for a routing table with overlapping prefixes predict which route is chosen (longest prefix, then metric) and verify with `ip route get`
Examine NAT/firewall policy — read an nftables ruleset and a NAT configuration, predict what happens to given packets (accepted, dropped, rewritten) and confirm with captures
Verify segmentation controls — write the intended policy between zones as a matrix, implement it with default deny, and prove every allowed and every denied flow with a test and a capture

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: in a DNS answer, what does the AA flag mean and what do the authority and additional sections hold? What distinguishes NXDOMAIN from SERVFAIL? How long does a negative answer live?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Routing is a lookup: the most specific matching prefix wins; ties are broken by metric; a default route matches everything. Return paths matter: a packet that arrives but whose reply has no route is a common "firewall" mystery.
- A stateful firewall tracks connections: replies to allowed outbound connections are accepted by state, so rules describe who may start a conversation. Order matters: the first matching rule decides, so a broad accept above a narrow drop defeats it.
- NAT rewrites addresses and ports and keeps a table to undo it. It changes what a capture shows on each side and is not a security boundary by itself.
- Segmentation means that every path between zones is listed and each is allowed or denied on purpose. Default deny with explicit allows is testable; default allow with exceptions is not.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. On `net-router` set up three zones (users, servers, management) as separate subnets.
2. Write the matrix first: which zone may start which connection to which port in which zone; everything else is denied.
3. Implement it in an nftables `forward` chain with policy drop, a rule accepting established and related traffic, one rule per allowed flow, and counters. Add source NAT for one zone going to an "outside" address and look at the entries with `conntrack -L`.
4. Prove every cell of the matrix with a connection attempt and read the counters; capture one allowed and one denied flow on both router interfaces and show the NAT rewrite.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Add a fourth zone (a DMZ) and extend the matrix. Prepare three flawed rulesets for it (an accept above a drop, a reply path with no route, a NAT rule that also rewrites management traffic). Draw one at random, predict its behaviour by reading it, then test your prediction and fix it with the smallest change.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Turn the matrix into an automated test: a script that tries every (source zone, destination zone, port) combination, compares the outcome with the matrix and prints a difference report. Run it on the correct ruleset, then change one rule and show that the script catches it. State what the test cannot show (for example paths through a host that bridges two zones).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the matrix (intended and observed), the ruleset with its hash, the counters, the two annotated captures, and the output of the test script before and after the planted change. It is accepted when every cell has an observed result and every difference is explained.

D10.watch_for: A rule that matches nothing because the interface name is wrong. Testing from the router itself, which bypasses the forward chain. Calling a flat test "segmentation verified".

D11.title: Scoped reconnaissance
objectives: Define reconnaissance scope — write the rules for a reconnaissance exercise on the lab: target list, permitted techniques and rate, forbidden actions, time window, data handling and stop condition, each tied to the day 1 authorization

Interpret discovery results — run host discovery and service and version detection against the lab subnets inside the scope and explain each result (open, closed, filtered, banner, operating-system guess) with its confidence and what could make it wrong
Translate observations into risks — turn the findings into a ranked list of risks with evidence, likelihood and impact reasoning, and say which findings are not yet risks

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what makes a zone boundary testable? Write the nftables ruleset order rule in one sentence. What does source NAT change in a capture on each side of the router?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Scope comes before the tool: who authorized what, which addresses and ports, which techniques (passive observation, host discovery, port scanning, version detection), at what rate, in what window, and what stops the exercise. A scan outside scope is an incident, not a mistake.
- Host discovery and port scanning are inferences from replies. A port is open if something answers, closed if a reset comes back, filtered if nothing useful does. Version detection and operating-system guesses are fingerprints: they compare observed behaviour with a database and can be wrong or spoofed.
- Scans have side effects: they fill logs, trip alarms and can crash fragile services. Rate and timing are part of the scope.
- Read the nmap reference guide on scan types, port states and timing; note which options need privileges.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write the scope document for the three lab subnets and sign it as owner. It lists targets, allowed techniques, a maximum rate, a time window, the evidence folder and the stop condition.
2. Within it: host discovery (`nmap -sn`), a full TCP port scan of one host (`-sS -p-`), then service and version detection on the open ports (`-sV`), saving all output formats (`-oA`). Capture the scan traffic from the target side.
3. Compare the scan results with ground truth from `ss -tulpn` on each target. List every difference (a filtered port you know is open, a banner that names the wrong version) and explain it.
4. Show in the capture what the scanner sent for one open, one closed and one filtered port.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three surprises on clones (a service on an unusual port, a port filtered by a firewall rule, a banner configured to lie) and a decoy host. Draw a random configuration, scan it within your scope, and reconstruct the real service map with a confidence for every line. Then reveal the truth and score yourself: which lines were wrong and which instrument would have corrected them.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a detection for the scan you just ran: from a capture or firewall log count distinct destination ports and hosts per source in a short window and alert above a threshold. Test it against a full port scan, a slow scan at a low rate and ordinary browsing; record what it catches and misses and tune it. State plainly what a slow scan does to your threshold.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the report: scope; method with every command; the results table with confidence and reasoning; the comparison with ground truth; the ranked risks (an open management port is a risk, an open web port is a fact until you know what it serves); limitations. It is accepted when each risk cites an observation and each unsure result says what would settle it.

D13.title: HTTP semantics and browser trust boundaries
objectives: Explain HTTP request semantics — for given requests predict method safety and idempotency, status code, caching and redirect behaviour, and verify each prediction against your own server with `curl -v`
Analyze cookies, origins and headers — read the cookie attributes, CORS headers and security headers of a response and state exactly what each allows or blocks in a browser, with a test for each
Map browser trust boundaries — draw the origins, frames, cookies and storage of a small multi-origin application and mark where the same-origin policy, CORS and a content security policy apply

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what are the two things a routing table lookup decides? Why is default allow with exceptions untestable as segmentation? Write the three parts of the scope statement you would need before scanning a web server.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A request has a method, a target, headers and an optional body; a response has a status, headers and a body. Safe methods do not change state, idempotent ones can be repeated with the same effect, and a server that changes state on GET breaks both promises. Read the sections of RFC 9110 on methods and status codes.
- An origin is scheme, host and port. The same-origin policy stops a page from reading another origin's responses; CORS is the server's way of relaxing that for named origins, and a wildcard origin with credentials is refused by browsers. A content security policy restricts what a page may load or run.
- A cookie is sent to every request that matches its domain and path unless attributes restrict it: `Secure` (HTTPS only), `HttpOnly` (not readable by page script), `SameSite` (cross-site sending). Read RFC 6265 and the cookie chapter of the OWASP testing guide.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write the lab application's first version: a login page, a notes list, a note page and an API route. Run it on two hostnames under `lab.test` (for example `a.lab.test` and `b.lab.test`).
2. With `curl -v` look at methods, status codes, caching headers and redirects. For five requests write the prediction first, then compare.
3. Set cookies with different attributes and show in the browser's developer tools which requests carry them. Test `SameSite` by loading a page from `b.lab.test` that submits a form to `a.lab.test`.
4. Make a page on `b.lab.test` read a response of `a.lab.test` with `fetch`: show the block, add CORS headers, show the preflight request for a non-simple request, then show that credentials need an explicit origin.
5. Add a content security policy that blocks inline script and show the console report.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare six response header sets (cookies, CORS, CSP, framing) and six browser scenarios that each ask "will this work?". Write your predictions, then run all thirty-six combinations or a random dozen, and score your predictions. For every wrong one, find which rule you mis-remembered.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a header audit in Python that fetches a list of URLs and reports cookies missing `Secure`, `HttpOnly` or `SameSite`, missing or weak CSP, framing allowed without a decision, a CORS wildcard with credentials, and missing `X-Content-Type-Options`. Run it on your application before and after you fix each finding and show it fails on the weak configuration and passes on the fixed one.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the annotated requests and responses with a predicted-versus-observed table, the origin and trust-boundary diagram, and the audit output before and after. It is accepted when each header on the diagram has a test that shows its effect in a browser.

D13.watch_for: Treating CORS as an access control for the server: it only changes what a browser lets a page read. Testing cookies over HTTP and wondering why `Secure` blocks them. Confusing site and origin.

D14.title: Authentication and session state
objectives: Model authentication/session state — draw the lifecycle of a session from login through use to logout and expiry, naming where each piece of state lives and what every transition must check

Analyze controlled session defects — find the planted defects in your own application (a predictable session identifier, no rotation at login, logout that does not invalidate, a session identifier in a URL, a weak password reset) and show evidence for each
Test session mitigations — implement and prove identifier rotation, secure cookie attributes, idle and absolute timeouts, server-side invalidation and rate limiting of login attempts

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which of `Secure`, `HttpOnly` and `SameSite` stops script from reading a cookie? What is an origin? Predict what a browser does with a response that sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Authentication proves who is asking; a session is the server's memory of that proof, carried by an identifier the client presents on each request. The identifier must be unguessable, bound to the server-side record, rotated when privilege changes (login, step-up) and destroyed on logout and expiry.
- Common defects: fixation (the attacker chooses the identifier and the server keeps it after login), identifiers in URLs, no server-side invalidation, long-lived tokens, passwords stored with a fast hash. Passwords are stored with a slow, salted, memory-hard scheme (Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt), never with a general-purpose hash.
- Login must resist guessing without letting an attacker lock out a victim: throttle per account and per source, with delays that grow.
- Read the OWASP cheat sheets on session management, authentication and password storage.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add login to the lab application with three planted defects on a branch: sequential session identifiers, no rotation at login, logout that only clears the cookie.
2. Show each defect with evidence: predict the next identifier from two observed ones; set an identifier before login and show it is still valid afterwards (fixation); replay a logged-out cookie and show it still works.
3. Fix each on its own commit and add a test per defect that fails before the fix.
4. Store passwords with a slow salted scheme and show with a timing measurement that verification takes the intended time.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: On the PortSwigger Web Security Academy, choose three authentication labs at random from the list without reading their titles first (a die and the list order will do). Solve them, noting for each the underlying flaw in one sentence, the tool you used and the time. Then write for each one the control that would have prevented it.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Implement login throttling: count failures per account and per source address, delay growing with the count, and a message that does not reveal whether the account exists. Test it with a script from `lin-aux` that tries a small list of synthetic passwords, show the delay engaging, show a legitimate login still works after the window, and discuss how an attacker could use your lockout against a victim and what you chose to do about it.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the lifecycle diagram, the evidence of each planted defect, the commit and test that closed it, the timing measurement and the throttling test log. It is accepted when every defect shows a failing test before and a passing test after.

D14.watch_for: Rotating the identifier but keeping the old one valid. Locking accounts so that anyone can lock anyone. Testing only the happy path of logout.

D15.title: Authorization and object-level access
objectives: Distinguish authentication/authorization — for ten endpoints state what the server must check (who is asking, may they do this, on this object) and where it checks today
Examine object access failure — find and demonstrate in the lab application an insecure direct object reference and a missing function-level check, and name the exact missing check
Build regression cases — write automated tests that fail while the flaw exists and pass after the fix, covering access to another user's objects and to administrative functions

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: draw the session lifecycle and mark the two moments the identifier must change. Why does `HttpOnly` not stop session fixation? State the rule for storing a password.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Authentication answers "who"; authorization answers "may this principal do this action on this object". The second question must be asked on every request, on the server, for every object, not once at login and not by hiding links.
- Horizontal failures reach another user's objects at the same privilege level (object-level, often called insecure direct object reference or broken object level authorization); vertical failures reach functions of a higher role (function-level). An unguessable identifier is not an authorization check.
- Defensible design: one central policy check that every route calls, deny by default, ownership derived from the session rather than from the request, and tests with at least two ordinary users and one administrator.
- Read the OWASP testing guide on authorization testing and the API security list's entries on object-level and function-level authorization.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add notes owned by users, a note page `/notes/ID`, an edit endpoint and an administrative page. Plant two defects on a branch: the note page checks login but not ownership, the administrative page is only linked for admins.
2. Create three accounts (two users, one admin). Demonstrate both defects with two sessions and `curl`.
3. Write the matrix before the fix (rows are roles and anonymous, columns are endpoints, cells are allowed or denied), then fill the observed column.
4. Fix with one central check, rerun the matrix, and commit the tests.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose three access-control labs at random from the Web Security Academy list and two access-control challenges from the OWASP Juice Shop. For each, state the missing check in one sentence and sketch the central policy that would make the class of flaw impossible.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a deny-by-default test: enumerate every route of your application, call each as anonymous, as user A, as user B and as admin, and compare with a policy table. The test must fail when a route has no entry in the table. Add a route without a policy and show the test fails; add the entry and show it passes.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the matrix with expected and observed results, a paragraph per difference naming the missing check, the central policy design, and the deny-by-default test output. It is accepted when every route appears in the matrix and the test fails on an unlisted route.

D15.watch_for: Checking the role but not the owner. Reading the owner from a request parameter. A test that only calls routes as the user who owns the data.

D16.title: Injection root causes
objectives: Explain injection root causes — explain how building a query or command from strings lets data become code, and where the parser boundary is, for SQL, shell and template contexts
Analyze vulnerable controlled fixture — find the injection point in your own application, demonstrate the behaviour with synthetic data and show the exact statement that results
Validate prepared statements — replace concatenation with parameters, prove the earlier inputs are inert, and state what parameters do not cover (identifiers, sort order, wildcards in `LIKE`)

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which of the two checks, who and may they, does a central policy answer? Name two ways an access-control test suite can miss a route. What is the difference between a horizontal and a vertical failure?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Injection exists wherever untrusted text is concatenated into something another parser will interpret: a SQL statement, a shell command line, a template, an LDAP filter. The fix is to keep code and data separate (parameters, argument lists, safe template contexts), not to try to clean the data.
- SQL classes: in-band (the result shows in the page), blind (the effect is inferred from behaviour or timing) and out-of-band. You need to recognize them; you do not need exploit code to defend against them.
- Parameters cannot carry identifiers or keywords. A column or sort order from a user must be matched against an allow-list.
- The database account should hold only the privileges the endpoint needs, so a flaw does less. ORMs still allow raw fragments; read their escape hatches.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. On a branch, add a search endpoint that builds its SQL by string formatting. Log every statement the database receives.
2. With synthetic data only, show three behaviours that prove the input reaches the parser: a quote that causes a syntax error, a condition that changes the number of rows returned, a boolean difference you can observe from outside. Record the statement that results each time.
3. Replace the concatenation with parameters. Re-run the same inputs and show they are treated as plain text.
4. Add a sort option and fix it with an allow-list.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose three SQL injection labs at random from the Web Security Academy list. For each, write the statement the application builds, the input that changes its meaning and the one-line fix. Then find one place in your own application that builds a shell command or a template from user input, and write the safe form.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Give the endpoint a database connection that can only read the table it needs (for SQLite, open the file read-only for read paths) and show that even with the vulnerable branch an injected write fails. Run a static analyser (Bandit or Semgrep with a rule for string-built SQL) on both branches, compare its findings with your tests, and record what it found that you missed and what it missed.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the explanation, the logged statements for each behaviour, the diff to parameters, the allow-list for sorting, the read-only evidence and the analyser comparison. It is accepted when each behaviour has a logged statement and each fix has a failing test before it.

D16.watch_for: Escaping quotes by hand. Parameterizing the value and concatenating the table name. A test whose "attack" string is mistyped and therefore proves nothing.

D17.title: Cross-site scripting contexts
objectives: Model XSS execution contexts — classify where untrusted data lands (HTML body, attribute, script string, URL, style, DOM sink) and which encoding or safe API each needs
Inspect controlled XSS — reproduce reflected, stored and DOM-based script execution in your own application with harmless markers and show where each runs

Verify context-sensitive output encoding — fix each context with the right encoding or a safe API, add a content security policy, and prove the earlier inputs are inert while legitimate input still renders

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name two things a parameter cannot carry. What privilege should a web application's database account have? Write one sentence explaining blind injection, and one reason string escaping by hand fails.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The same text is safe in one context and dangerous in another. In HTML body text the dangerous characters are `<` and `&`; in a quoted attribute the quote; in a JavaScript string the quote and backslash and the closing script tag; in a URL the scheme. Encoding must match the context in which the output lands, at the point of output.
- Reflected, stored and DOM-based differ in where the data comes from and where it is written. DOM sinks such as `innerHTML` and `document.write` parse HTML; `textContent` does not.
- Frameworks escape by default and offer escape hatches (marking a value safe); the hatches are where the defects are. A strict content security policy with nonces limits what an injected script can do; `HttpOnly` limits what it can steal. Neither makes the output safe.
- Read the OWASP cheat sheets on cross-site scripting prevention and DOM-based XSS prevention.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add three features on a branch: a search page that echoes the query, a comment list that stores and shows comments, a page that writes a URL fragment into the document with `innerHTML`.
2. Use a harmless marker (a script that changes the page title) to show each runs. Record in which context the marker landed in each.
3. Fix each with the right tool: context-aware template escaping, `textContent` for the DOM case, an allow-list sanitizer for the one place where limited HTML must be allowed.
4. Re-run the markers and also a set of legitimate inputs (names with apostrophes, angle brackets in code samples) to show nothing legitimate broke.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose three cross-site scripting labs at random from the Web Security Academy list. For each, write the context, why the first attempt failed, and the encoding that would have stopped it. Then review your own application's templates and list every place that disables escaping.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Add a content security policy that forbids inline script and allows scripts only by nonce. Deploy it first in report-only mode, collect the violations, fix them, then enforce it. Show that the earlier stored marker is blocked even on the vulnerable branch, and list what the policy does not stop (for example injection into an allowed script's data).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the context table with one example per context, the three reproductions, the fixes and the legitimate-input tests, and the policy with its violation log. It is accepted when each fix has a failing test before it and the legitimate inputs still render.

D17.watch_for: Encoding for the wrong context. Sanitizing on input and trusting the stored value everywhere. Judging success by a popup instead of by the context.

D18.title: Week 3 assessment (blind practical)
objectives: Analyze blind web task — review an unfamiliar web application for the week's classes of defect and report each with a reproduction
Diagnose security failure — separate symptom from cause for each finding, naming the missing check, the unsafe construction or the wrong output context
Verify remediation and document evidence — fix each defect with the smallest change, prove it with a test that failed before, and record the evidence with hashes

sections.name: Blind practical
sections.markdown: Open the assessment in the application, start the attempt and read the task statement. Take the application from the source you fixed before the week and do not read its code or its list of defects before the clock starts. Stop at 120 minutes.

sections.name: Remediation
sections.markdown: Grade yourself against the rubric before reading any answer key. For every criterion below your target, find the cause in your method (which class of defect you did not test for, which request you did not replay as a second user) and fix the gap with a short targeted exercise on your own lab application. Then redo the part that failed on a different instance.

sections.name: Report
sections.markdown: Write the report in the structure of the task statement: findings ordered by impact, each with reproduction, root cause, fix, regression test and verification; what you did not test. Attach the evidence with SHA-256 values.

sections.name: Performance review
sections.markdown: Compare the grade with the week's targets: independent execution, a second user used for every access test, root cause rather than symptom, regression tests that fail before the fix, evidence quality, honest limits. Record the three habits that cost you most and one change for next week.

D18.watch_for: Testing every endpoint as the same user. Stopping at the first finding. A fix with no test that failed before it.
