D19.title: API identity, tokens and object-level authorization
objectives: Map API token/identity flow — draw how an API authenticates callers (API key, session cookie, OAuth 2.0 access token, signed token), what each credential asserts, who validates it and how it is revoked
Check object-level authorization — test every object-bearing route of a small REST API with two tenants and several roles and record which checks are missing at object, property and function level

Define API tests — write an automated suite for authentication failure modes (no token, expired, wrong audience, wrong signing algorithm) and for authorization (cross-tenant access, mass assignment, excessive data in responses)

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the classes of defect you fixed last week and name the test that guards each. What does `HttpOnly` protect and what does it not? Name the three cookie attributes.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- An API key identifies an application, not a person. An OAuth 2.0 access token is a bearer credential: whoever holds it can use it, so audience, scope, lifetime and storage matter. A signed token (JWT) is verified by checking its signature, the algorithm you expect (never the one the token names), issuer, audience and expiry. Read RFC 6749, RFC 6750, RFC 7519 and the best-practice RFC 8725.
- The API security list names the recurring failures: object-level authorization, broken authentication, object-property-level authorization (which covers both returning too much and accepting writes to fields the caller must not set, called mass assignment) and function-level authorization.
- Authorization lives on the server per request, per object, per property. Schemas (an OpenAPI description, response models) make the allowed shape explicit and testable.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Build the lab API with `POST /login` returning a signed token, `GET /accounts/ID`, `PATCH /accounts/ID` and an administrative route. Two tenants, users with roles.
2. Write the matrix first, then the tests: no token gives 401; expired, wrong audience, wrong signature and a token whose header asks for no signature are all refused; a user of tenant A reading tenant B's account is refused; a `PATCH` that includes a `role` field does not change the role; the response never contains the password hash.
3. Run the tests against a deliberately weak first version (it should fail several), then fix one defect per commit.
4. Fill in the observed column of the matrix from the test results.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Run the OWASP crAPI in its containers on the lab network. Choose three of its challenges at random from the list without reading the titles first. For each, record the request that shows the flaw, the class from the API security list, and the check that was missing. Write the test you would add to its code base.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Make the response shape explicit: serializers with an allow-list of fields per role, input models that reject unknown fields, and a per-token rate limit. Prove with tests that a client cannot read a field it should not see, cannot write a field it should not set, and is throttled after a burst. Show that hiding a field in the client would not have passed the same tests.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the matrix with the name of the test for every cell, the three crAPI notes, and the diff that introduced the allow-lists. It is accepted when every route appears in the matrix and every cell is backed by a test that fails on the weak version.

D19.watch_for: Accepting the algorithm named in the token. Checking the tenant on read and not on update. Filtering a field in the client and calling it protected.

D20.title: Server-side request forgery
objectives: Explain SSRF trust boundary — explain how a server that fetches a user-supplied address can be made to reach internal services and metadata endpoints, and which network and application trust assumptions this breaks
Analyze isolated SSRF scenario — add a preview-by-URL feature to the lab application, show it reaching an internal-only service you host, and map what a caller learns at each step

Verify destination restrictions — implement and test allow-listing after name resolution, redirect handling, scheme and port limits and network egress rules, and show the bypass classes you tried are refused

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what is the difference between a token's audience and its issuer? Why is a client-side filter not a control? List the four checks of a validated signed token.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A server that makes requests on behalf of a user acts with the server's network position, which usually sees more than the user does: internal admin pages, databases, and on cloud hosts a metadata service on a link-local address. SSRF is the abuse of that position.
- Validation by string is weak. Addresses have many spellings, hostnames resolve to different addresses at different times (a hostname can resolve to a public address when checked and to an internal one when used), redirects change the destination after the check, and IPv6 and mapped addresses reach the same machines.
- Layered defence: an allow-list of destinations, resolve once and connect to the checked address, no redirects or revalidation on each, only `http` and `https` on stated ports, refusal of loopback, private, link-local and unique-local ranges after resolution, the response not returned raw, and egress rules so the web host cannot reach internal services it does not need.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add `/preview?url=` to the lab application using a plain HTTP client. Put an internal service on the other subnet that returns a recognisable banner and is reachable only from the web host.
2. Show the application fetching the internal banner for the caller. Map what the caller can learn: whether a port is open, how long it took, what the response says.
3. Write a validator that resolves the name, checks the address against the refused ranges and connects to that address. Write tests for alternate spellings of the loopback and private addresses (decimal, octal, short forms, IPv6 and mapped forms), for a redirect to an internal address, and for a name that you make resolve differently on a second lookup in your lab DNS.
4. Run the tests against the naive and the fixed validator and keep the failing output of the first.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose three server-side request forgery labs at random from the Web Security Academy list. For each, record the sink, the check that existed and why it failed, and the one change that would have stopped it. Then list every feature of your own application that makes an outbound request and rate the destination control of each.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Add the network layer: an egress rule on the web guest that denies private destinations except an explicit list. Prove that an SSRF attempt which gets past your validator on the naive branch is still stopped at the network, and that the application's legitimate outbound call still works. State what the layers together still do not stop.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the diagram (the application, the internal service, the allowed and refused flows), the demonstration, the test list by bypass class with failing and passing output, and the egress rule with its test. It is accepted when every bypass class has a test and the network rule is shown to work independently of the validator.

D20.watch_for: Validating the hostname and then letting the library resolve it again. Blocking `127.0.0.1` and forgetting `::1`. A redirect that moves the request after your check.

D21.title: Uploads and unsafe deserialization
objectives: Evaluate upload validation — test an upload feature for trust in the declared type and the file name, path traversal in names, oversized and compressed-bomb inputs and the risk of stored files being executed, and decide what to allow

Explain unsafe deserialization — explain why reading untrusted data with a format that can create arbitrary objects lets the data choose the code that runs, and show a harmless proof in a sandboxed guest
Build input-processing tests — write tests with hostile fixtures for the upload and the importer that fail on the unsafe version and pass on the safe one

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list three bypass classes for an SSRF filter and say which layer stops each. Why does connecting to the checked address matter? What did your egress rule block?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Uploads: the browser's declared type and the file name are attacker-controlled. Decide by content (the leading bytes), allow only the types you need, generate the stored name yourself, store outside the web root on a mount that cannot execute, set a size limit while streaming, re-encode images, and serve user content with a download disposition and `nosniff`. Archives add path traversal in member names and expansion bombs.
- Deserialization: some formats can rebuild arbitrary objects and call code while doing so (Python `pickle`, Java native serialization, YAML tags that construct objects). Untrusted input must use a data-only format (JSON with a schema). A signature does not make an unsafe format safe if the key can leak.
- Read the cheat sheets on file upload and on deserialization; read the page of your language's documentation that warns about the unsafe module.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add an avatar upload that trusts the declared type and uses the supplied file name, and a settings import that reads a serialized object.
2. In the sandbox guest show the file name traversal writing a harmless marker file outside the upload directory, and a file with a lying type accepted. Do not upload anything that runs.
3. For the importer, show with a harmless marker (an object that makes the process create a file named `marker`) that data selected the code. Then replace it with JSON and a schema.
4. Fix the upload: content check, allow-list, generated name, size limit while streaming.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose three labs at random from the Web Security Academy's file upload and insecure deserialization topics. For each, write the sink, the missing control and the fix. Then write the hostile fixture set for your own features: a file with a double extension, a path in the name, a huge file, a nested archive and a deeply nested document.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Contain the damage: mount the upload directory with `noexec,nosuid,nodev`, run the service under a systemd unit that limits where it can write, and show a script placed in the upload directory cannot be executed through the service. Add the fixtures as tests that fail on the naive code and pass on yours.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the review of each feature (what is accepted, what is refused and why), the sandbox demonstrations, the fixtures with failing and passing output and the containment evidence. It is accepted when every refused input has a test and the containment is shown with a command and its output.

D21.watch_for: Trusting the extension, the declared type or both. A "safe" loader that still allows object tags. Testing the validator with one file instead of a set that tries to break it.

D22.title: Business logic and concurrency
objectives: Assess business logic invariants — list the invariants of a small shop workflow (a balance never below zero, a coupon used once, stock never negative, only legal state transitions) and find where the code relies on the client or on call order to keep them

Examine controlled concurrency issue — reproduce a race (double redemption of a coupon, overdrawing a balance) with parallel requests against your application and show the interleaving that breaks the invariant

Create race-condition regression — fix it with a database constraint, an atomic update or a transaction at a suitable isolation level, and add a test that runs the parallel scenario repeatedly and fails on the unsafe version

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: why is a content type not evidence of what a file is? Name the two mount options that stop execution and the setuid effect. What does the safe replacement for a pickle import look like?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A business rule is an invariant, a statement that must hold after every operation. Validation at the edge is not enforcement: the rule must be enforced where the state lives, by constraints and atomic operations, because requests interleave.
- Check-then-act is the classic race: read the balance, test it, write the new one. Two requests can both read before either writes. Fixes: a single atomic statement (`UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - x WHERE balance >= x`), a uniqueness constraint, row locking, a version column checked on update, or serializable transactions with a retry.
- Logic abuse also includes tampered prices and quantities (negative values), skipped steps in a workflow, and replaying a request; an idempotency key defends the last.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add a wallet, a coupon that may be redeemed once, and a checkout. Write the invariants first as a list with a query that checks each.
2. Plant check-then-act in coupon redemption. Fire twenty parallel redemptions from a script and show more than one succeeds; show the log of the interleaving.
3. Fix it three ways on three commits (unique constraint, atomic update, transaction with retry) and compare the behaviour under the same load.
4. Add tests for a negative quantity, a price sent by the client, a skipped payment step and a replayed order.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose three labs at random from the Web Security Academy's business logic and race condition topics. For each, state the invariant that was violated and where it should have been enforced. Then review your own application for any rule that depends on the order in which the client calls endpoints.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write an invariant monitor that runs the queries from step 1 against the database and alerts on any violation. Run it after hammering the unsafe version (it must flag the damage) and the safe version (it must be silent). Add a detection for the attack pattern itself, many near-simultaneous redemptions of one coupon from one session, and say what it cannot see.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the invariants with their checking queries, the interleaving evidence, the three fixes with their results under load, and the monitor output on both versions. It is accepted when each invariant has a query and the race test fails on the unsafe version more often than not.

D22.watch_for: A test that sends requests one after another and calls it concurrency. Fixing the symptom with a lock that does not span processes. A constraint added in the application but not in the database.

D23.title: Application threat model
objectives: Draft application data-flow model — draw the data-flow diagram of the lab application with trust boundaries, assets, entry points and data stores, derived from the code and the running system rather than from memory
Rank vulnerabilities — enumerate threats per element, score each by likelihood and impact on a stated scale, and justify the ordering with evidence from weeks 3 and 4
Verify mitigations — for the five highest threats state the mitigation, the test that shows it works and the residual risk, and run the tests

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the invariants of your wallet workflow and the statement that enforces each. Name three fixes for check-then-act. Which of them survives two application processes?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Threat modelling answers four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, and did we do a good enough job. The artefact is a diagram, a list of threats and a list of actions with owners, and it is updated when the system changes.
- A data-flow diagram has external entities, processes, data stores, flows and trust boundaries; threats are found where a flow crosses a boundary. STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege) is a checklist for each element.
- Rank with a stated scale for likelihood and for impact and write the reasoning; a score with no evidence is an opinion. Tie each threat to a requirement and to a test, so the model is checked by the build.
- Read the OWASP threat modelling cheat sheet and the application security verification standard's structure.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Derive the diagram from the system: list every route, every outbound call and every data store from the code and from `ss`, and place the trust boundaries (browser, web host, internal service, database).
2. For each element and boundary crossing, write the STRIDE threats that apply. Strike the ones the system already stops, citing the control and test.
3. Score the rest with your stated scale and rank them. For the top five write mitigation, test and residual risk.
4. Keep the model in git as text (a diagram in a text format and a table).

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Build a threat model of a different application, the OWASP Juice Shop or crAPI, in ninety minutes using only its running behaviour and documentation. Compare its top five with the list of its known challenges afterwards and score your recall: what did you find, what did you miss, and which element of your method would have found it.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Turn the top five mitigations into automated checks in your repository (a `make security` target running `pytest` tests and the header audit of day 13). Run it. Remove one mitigation and show the target fails. State which threats in the model remain without an automated check and why.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the threat model: diagram, threat table with scores and reasoning, the five mitigations with their tests, residual risks, the independent-lab comparison and the check target's output with and without the removed mitigation. It is accepted when every ranked threat cites evidence and every top-five mitigation has a test that fails without it.

D23.watch_for: A diagram drawn from memory. Scores with no reasoning. A model nobody updates after the next change.

D25.title: Windows principals, services and event records
objectives: Model Windows principals/services — draw the principals of a Windows host (users, groups, security identifiers, service accounts, virtual accounts, the system account) and the services that run as each, with the privileges and token groups that follow
Interpret event records — read logon, special-privilege, process-creation and service-installation events, with the right auditing enabled, and reconstruct what a session did

Map privilege boundaries — mark where one principal can act as another (service control, impersonation, scheduled tasks, remote procedure endpoints) and which of those boundaries the vendor treats as a security boundary

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which setting of a sudo rule makes it unsafe, and which capability would you refuse on an interpreter? List five places a host can be made to run code at boot. Which of your week 4 mitigations had a test that failed without it?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Every principal has a security identifier. A process runs with an access token that lists the user, the groups, the privileges (enabled or not) and an integrity level. Services run under accounts chosen by their configuration: the system account, the local service and network service accounts, virtual accounts, or a named account.
- Auditing is off for much of what matters until you turn it on: logon and logoff, special privileges assigned to a new logon, process creation (with the command line), and service installation each have their own policy and event. System Monitor (Sysmon) adds process, network, file and registry events with a configuration of your choice.
- The vendor's servicing criteria state which boundaries it defends (for example between user mode and kernel, or between sessions) and which are conveniences (for example elevation prompts).
- Read the Windows security documentation on access tokens and logon types and the Sysmon page.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. In the Windows guest enable advanced audit policy for logon, special logon, process creation with command-line logging, and security system extension (service installation). Install Sysmon with a configuration you have read line by line.
2. Create a local user, a group, a virtual-account service and a service under a named account. For each running service list the account and the privileges (`whoami /all` run as that account, `sc qc`, Process Explorer's token view).
3. Perform a short scripted session as the new user (log on, start a program, install a benign service, create a scheduled task). Collect the events and write the session's timeline with the event numbers.
4. Draw the principals-and-services diagram and mark, for each arrow, whether the boundary is a security boundary or a convenience, with your reason.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three benign session scripts on three clones (each performs a different mix of logon, process start, account change, service and task creation) and discard the scripts' text. Draw one at random and reconstruct what happened from the event logs alone. Then replay your reconstruction against the script and score it: what you got right, what the logs could not show.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a PowerShell script that verifies the audit configuration is present (reads the policy, then proves it by generating a logon, a process start and a service installation and finding the events). Run it on the guest before and after you disable one policy and show it reports the gap. Add a summary of logon type and source for each successful logon in the last day.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the diagram with boundary classification, the timeline of the session with event numbers, the auditing configuration and the verification output. It is accepted when every statement in the timeline cites an event and the diagram's classifications each carry a reason.

D25.watch_for: Reading a logon event without its logon type. Assuming command-line auditing is on. Calling a prompt a boundary because it feels like one.

D26.title: Linux privilege boundaries
objectives: Explain sudo/capabilities/service permissions — explain how sudo rules, file capabilities, setuid files and service sandboxing each grant or limit privilege and what a given rule really allows

Analyze controlled Linux misconfiguration — find in a prepared guest the planted privilege paths (a sudo rule that allows an editor or interpreter, a writable file run by root, a capability on an interpreter, a setuid helper) and show in the lab how each would let a low-privilege user act as root
Verify hardening — remove each path with the smallest change and prove as the low-privilege user that it no longer works while the legitimate task still does

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what does a Windows service's account decide? Name three events that record a service being created or a user gaining special privileges. What is the difference between a privilege and an access right?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Root is a user identity with the kernel's permission checks bypassed; capabilities split that power into units, and a process or a file can hold some without being root. A setuid program runs with its owner's identity; one that can be made to start a shell or write a file is a path to root.
- A sudo rule is a grant of "run this command as that user". Wildcards, commands that can start other programs (editors, pagers, interpreters), environment settings that are kept, and writable directories on the command's path all widen it. Read the sudoers manual and keep a list of "commands that can break out" such as the GTFOBins catalogue.
- Privileged programs that execute files others can write (cron jobs, systemd units, scripts found through `PATH`) hand their identity to whoever can write the file.
- Containers change the picture: root in a container is not root on the host only if the configuration holds.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Build `lin-priv` from `clean-0` with four planted paths: a sudo rule for an editor, a root-owned cron script that is writable by a group your user belongs to, a file capability on a scripting interpreter, a setuid copy of a helper that starts programs.
2. As the low-privilege user find each with `sudo -l`, `find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null`, `getcap -r / 2>/dev/null` and a review of root's scheduled jobs. For each, write why it works, then show in the lab, with a harmless marker (a file created by root), that it does.
3. Fix each with the smallest change: restrict the sudo rule to a fixed command, correct the file mode, remove the capability, remove the setuid bit or the program.
4. Re-run the discovery commands and the markers as the low-privilege user.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three more guests, each with two paths drawn from a list you wrote, and draw one at random. Find the paths without reading the list, using enumeration commands and logic only. For each, record the evidence, the reason it works and the fix. Then spend thirty minutes on the OverTheWire Bandit levels that involve cron and setuid programs and note how the same reasoning applies.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write an audit script that reports sudo rules that allow shells or interpreters, setuid and setgid files, file capabilities, files executed by cron or systemd that are writable by anyone but their owner, and world-writable directories on root's `PATH`. Run it on the planted guest (it must report all four paths) and on the fixed guest (it must be quiet for them), and compare with the baseline of day 1.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the four paths with their reasons and evidence, the fixes, the before and after outputs of your audit, and the markers as proof. It is accepted when each path has a one-sentence reason it works and a test as the low-privilege user that fails after the fix.

D26.watch_for: Testing as root, which finds nothing. A fix that removes the demonstration but not the reason. A sudo rule fixed for the command but not for its arguments.

D27.title: Windows tokens and service controls
objectives: Analyze Windows token/service controls — explain how access tokens, privileges, integrity levels and service configuration (account, access control list, binary path, recovery actions) determine what a process can do

Investigate controlled privilege failure — find in a prepared Windows guest the planted weaknesses (an unquoted service path, a service directory writable by users, a service whose configuration users may change, a service account holding a dangerous privilege) and show the effect in the lab
Document remediation/detection — for each weakness write the fix, the test that proves it and the event or telemetry that would show its abuse

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: draw the privilege paths of your Linux guest in one sentence each. Which of them needed a writable file and which a command allowed by sudo? Write the command that lists file capabilities.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A token carries privileges such as the ability to impersonate another user or to debug processes; service accounts often hold some by design. A privilege that lets a process act with another principal's identity makes any flaw in that process a path to higher privilege.
- A service is a configuration: account, binary path, start type, an access control list on the service object, and access control lists on the files and directories it runs from. If a path with spaces is not quoted, Windows tries shorter names first; if a low-privilege user can write to any directory it passes through, or can change the service's configuration, the user chooses what the service account runs.
- Controls: quote paths, tighten directory and service access control lists, run services as the least privileged account that works (virtual accounts or managed service accounts), restrict what may run (application control in audit mode first), remove unneeded privileges.
- Read the documentation on access tokens, service security and access rights, and the AccessChk page.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Create two services on the Windows guest, one with an unquoted path under a directory with a space and a directory writable by a normal user, and one whose service object grants a normal user the right to change its configuration. Use a harmless program that writes its own identity to a file.
2. As a normal user enumerate with `sc qc`, `icacls` and `accesschk` and find both weaknesses without being told. Show the effect: the service account runs your harmless program.
3. Fix both: quote and relocate, tighten the access control lists, change the account. Repeat the enumeration and the demonstration and show they fail.
4. Turn on application control in audit mode, run the harmless program and find the audit events.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three variants on clones (a service on a user-writable path, a scheduled task running a writable script, a service account with an unneeded privilege). Draw one at random. Enumerate as a normal user using only built-in tools and the Sysinternals set, state the weakness and the evidence, then fix it. Record how long the enumeration took and what you would automate.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a PowerShell audit that lists services with unquoted paths containing spaces, services running as accounts outside an allow-list, binary directories writable by non-administrators, and service access control entries that grant low-privilege groups configuration rights. Run it on the weak and fixed guests. Add the detection: the events and the Sysmon registry events that would show a service's path or account changing, and test that they appear.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the enumeration output as the normal user, the three weaknesses with the harmless-program evidence, the fixes, the audit output before and after, and the telemetry for each. It is accepted when each weakness shows evidence before and a failing demonstration after.

D27.watch_for: Fixing the path and leaving the writable directory. Testing as an administrator. An audit that cannot read the access control lists it is judging.

D28.title: Persistence mechanisms and telemetry
objectives: Map common persistence mechanisms — catalogue where code can be made to run again after a restart or a logon on Windows and Linux (autostart keys and folders, services, scheduled tasks and timers, shell profiles, SSH keys, event subscriptions) and tie each to its technique name in a public knowledge base
Identify associated telemetry — for each mechanism state the log, event or file change that records its creation and use, whether it is on by default and what must be configured
Propose detection checks — write a baseline-and-compare check for five mechanisms that reports new or changed entries and test it by creating a benign instance of each

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which two unquoted-path conditions must hold for a service weakness to be usable? What does a virtual account give you over the system account? Name the events you would expect when a service is installed.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Persistence is any way of making code run again without the actor returning. The same places are used legitimately: that is why the baseline matters. Windows: run keys, the startup folder, services, scheduled tasks, event subscriptions in the management instrumentation. Linux: systemd units and timers, cron, shell profile files, SSH authorized keys, preload files and udev rules.
- A public knowledge base of adversary techniques (ATT&CK) names these, groups them under the persistence tactic, and describes how each can be detected (since release v18, October 2025, through detection strategies and the log sources behind them; earlier releases listed data sources). Use it for vocabulary and coverage, not as a checklist to tick.
- Telemetry exists only if enabled: object-access and registry auditing, Sysmon registry and file events, the audit subsystem with watches on the right paths, file integrity monitoring. Know which of your hosts log which mechanism today and which silently do not.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. On both guests create one benign instance of five mechanisms each (for example a run key, a scheduled task, a service, a systemd timer, an SSH key). Each writes a marker when it fires.
2. Find the creation of each in the telemetry. Where nothing was recorded, say why and enable the source.
3. Reboot or log on again and confirm each fired.
4. Fill in the visibility matrix for every mechanism you listed, with the technique name next to each.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three clones, each with three hidden benign persistence entries drawn from mechanisms you chose, and hide the list. Draw one clone at random and find all three using enumeration tools and logs only. Record what found each, what you almost missed and which mechanism your enumeration did not cover at all.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Extend the drift check of day 1 into five persistence checks: unit and timer files, cron entries, shell profiles and authorized keys on Linux; run keys, scheduled tasks and services on Windows. Create a new benign instance of each after the baseline and show every check reports it; show the checks are silent on an unchanged host; name the mechanism you could not cover and why.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the matrix, the evidence of each creation event, the five checks with their before and after output, and the list of mechanisms with no telemetry. It is accepted when each cell of the matrix is backed by an observation or says "no telemetry", and each check has been shown to fire.

D29.title: Hardened baseline
objectives: Establish hardened baseline — define a hardened configuration for a Linux and a Windows guest from a published benchmark, record it as testable checks and apply it
Prioritize host weaknesses — assess the guests against the baseline, group the failures by the risk they carry in your lab, and justify an order of repair with evidence
Test configuration controls — for ten chosen settings prove the setting is in effect by a behavioural test and not only by reading the configuration

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name the five persistence mechanisms you checked and the telemetry for each. Which of your five checks would have missed the mechanism you did not cover? What does a baseline let you tell apart?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A hardening baseline is a published, reviewable list of settings with a rationale (the CIS benchmarks, the DISA security technical implementation guides, the vendor's security baselines). Use one as a source of checks, not as a goal: every setting has a cost, and an applied setting that breaks the service will be undone.
- Prioritize by the risk in context: exposure (is the service reachable), privilege (what does a compromise give), and ease (does it need a user or only a network). Order the repairs, do the high-risk ones first, record the ones you accept and why.
- A setting is proven by behaviour: ask the service to do the forbidden thing and see it refuse. A setting that is only read from a file may not be in effect (overridden, not reloaded, wrong scope).
- Scanners (Lynis, OpenSCAP) give breadth and a first list; they do not replace a test you wrote and understood.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Pick a published benchmark for your Linux guest and one for the Windows guest. Choose forty checks that apply to your lab and record each as a check with an expected result.
2. Run a scanner (Lynis or OpenSCAP on Linux, a vendor baseline comparison on Windows) and your checks against the unhardened guests. Group the failures by risk and write the order of repair with reasons.
3. Apply the first twenty. Re-run and record what changed and what broke.
4. Choose ten settings and write a behavioural test for each: for example refuse a root login over the network, refuse a password login, fail to run a program from the temporary directory, refuse an unsigned script, find a blocked legacy protocol.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Harden a third guest of a different release with the same baseline using only your checks and tests. Compare it with the first: which settings differed, which tests failed first time, which checks you had to rewrite. Update your tests so they run on both.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Turn the ten behavioural tests into a suite that runs in a minute (`pytest` for Linux, Pester or PowerShell for Windows). Run it on the hardened and unhardened guests. Update the day 1 drift check to the new baseline and show it reports a change to one hardened setting. Record what the suite cannot tell you (for example whether a setting would survive an update).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the check list with results before and after, the ranked failures with reasoning, the accepted risks, the behavioural tests and their output, and the updated drift check. It is accepted when each of the ten settings has a test that fails on the unhardened guest and passes on the hardened one.

D31.title: Forest, domain and trust model
objectives: Explain forest/domain/trust model — explain the roles of forest, domain, domain controller, global catalog, site and trust, and why the forest rather than the domain is the security boundary
Model principal relationships — model the users, groups (nesting and scope), computers and service accounts of the lab domain and their relationships as a graph
Identify identity trust boundaries — mark where trust crosses (trusts, replication, delegation, administrative tiers), state which way trust flows and what security identifier filtering changes

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which mechanism in last week's visibility matrix had no telemetry, and what would you enable to record it? What did your baseline check report that surprised you? Why does a hardening setting need a behavioural test?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A forest is the top of an Active Directory deployment: a shared schema, configuration and global catalog, with one or more domains in trees. Domain controllers replicate the directory within a domain and the configuration across the forest. A domain is an administrative and replication unit; the vendor's position is that the forest is the security boundary, because an administrator of any domain can reach the shared parts.
- A trust lets principals of one domain be authenticated for resources of another. It has a direction (the trusting domain trusts the trusted one), may be transitive, and can be filtered or limited (security identifier filtering, selective authentication).
- Groups have scopes (domain local, global, universal) and nest; effective membership is the transitive closure. The tiered administration model separates control of the domain controllers and identity systems (tier 0) from servers (tier 1) and workstations (tier 2) and forbids credentials of a higher tier on a lower one.
- Read the vendor documentation on the directory service, on trusts and on the enterprise access model.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Promote the first server to a domain controller of a new forest `corp.lab.test`. Create organisational units for the three tiers, ten users, six groups with nesting (including a group `Lab-Tier0` that stands in for domain administrators), two service accounts and the three computers. Join the member server and the client.
2. Enumerate with the Active Directory module and export users, groups, memberships and computers to files.
3. Write a Python script that reads the export, builds the membership graph, and reports the effective members of `Lab-Tier0` (the transitive closure) and every path by which a user is a member.
4. Draw the model with the trust and tier boundaries and state, for each boundary, what crosses it and who can cross.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Design, on paper and then in the lab as far as memory allows, a layout for a company with a head office, a subsidiary and an acquired company that must keep its own administrators. Decide forests, domains and trusts, the direction of each trust and whether to filter or limit it, and justify each as a statement about who is allowed to authenticate where. If the hardware allows, build a second small forest and a one-way trust and test authentication across it with selective authentication on and off.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Add tier checks to your script and to the event logs: report any member of `Lab-Tier0` who has logged on to a tier 1 or tier 2 computer (from the logon events), and any privileged group member outside an approved list. Plant one violation of each kind in the lab and show both reports find it and stay silent on the clean domain.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the diagram with boundaries and trust directions, the exports and the closure output, the tier checks with their before and after output, and the design of the three-company layout with its reasons. It is accepted when every boundary on the diagram states who can cross it and every effective member of `Lab-Tier0` is explained.

D31.watch_for: Treating a domain as a security boundary. Counting only direct members of a privileged group. Building the model from the names in the console instead of from the exported data.

D32.title: Kerberos issuance and validation
objectives: Explain Kerberos issuance/validation — explain who issues and validates each ticket (ticket-granting ticket, service ticket), what is encrypted with whose key, what the privilege attribute data carries, and what pre-authentication prevents
Interpret auth events — correlate the ticket and logon events on the domain controller and on the service host with the messages in a capture

Diagnose controlled ticket failure — from a symptom find the cause of a planted failure (clock skew, a missing or duplicate service principal name, a service account whose password changed, a wrong encryption type)

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what makes a trust one-way and what does the arrow mean? List the three group scopes. Which tier may a tier 0 credential touch?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The client proves its identity to the key distribution centre (on the domain controller) and receives a ticket-granting ticket encrypted with the domain's ticket-granting key. It presents that to request a service ticket for a named service, encrypted with the service account's key; the service decrypts it and learns who the client is and which groups, from the privilege attribute data inside. The client never sees the key of the service and the service never contacts the domain controller to verify.
- Pre-authentication makes the client prove knowledge of its key before a ticket is issued. Ticket lifetime, renewal, clock skew (five minutes by default) and encryption types (the AES types, and the older RC4) are configuration and are where most failures come from. Names that identify services (service principal names) must be unique and must be registered on the account that runs the service.
- Read RFC 4120 for the protocol and the vendor documentation of the protocol's extensions for the Windows behaviour.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Capture the traffic between the client, the domain controller and the member server while the client opens a file share. Identify the authentication service exchange, the ticket-granting exchange and the application exchange; annotate realm, client name, service name, encryption types and flags.
2. On the client inspect the ticket cache (`klist`). On the controller and the member server find the events for the ticket requests and the logon and match each to a message in the capture.
3. Register a service principal name for a test service and show the ticket request for it. Then break things one at a time: move the client's clock ten minutes, register a duplicate name, change the service account's password without updating the service, restrict the encryption types. For each, record the symptom, the error in the capture and the event, and the repair.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three failures on restored snapshots and draw one at random. Starting from "the file share asks for a password again", find the cause with the capture, the events and `setspn` only. Write the order in which you ruled hypotheses out and what finally settled it. Repeat with a second failure and a different tool.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Harden the domain's Kerberos: require the AES types, give service accounts long random passwords or use managed service accounts, and confirm services keep working. Write a query over the ticket events that lists service tickets issued with the older encryption type, and show it finds a request you forced and is empty after the hardening.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the annotated capture, the events matched to messages, the failure table (symptom, error, cause, repair) with your own captures, and the hardening evidence. It is accepted when each message of the exchange is matched to an event and each failure shows its error in a capture or log.

D32.watch_for: Diagnosing from the first error message without the capture. Duplicate service names on two accounts. Forgetting that a changed password changes the key the service tickets are encrypted with.

D33.title: Delegation types and excessive permissions
objectives: Examine delegation types — explain unconstrained, constrained and resource-based constrained delegation, what each lets a service do with a client's identity, and how to find each in a directory

Analyze excessive permissions — review the access control lists of privileged users, groups and computers for rights that let a lower-privileged principal change them, and the group nesting that grants them indirectly
Specify controls — for each finding write the control (remove, restrict, replace, protect) and the check that proves it, in a form someone else can apply

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: draw the Kerberos exchange and mark the key each message is encrypted with. What does clock skew do, and what is the default tolerance? Why must a service name be unique?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Delegation lets a service act toward other services with a client's identity. Unconstrained delegation makes the service hold the forwardable ticket-granting tickets of every client that authenticates to it, so a compromised host becomes every one of those clients. Constrained delegation limits the target services (and may allow the service to obtain tickets for a user who never authenticated to it). Resource-based delegation moves the decision to the target, which names who may delegate to it.
- Accounts can be protected: marked as sensitive and not delegable, placed in the protected users group; the machine account quota controls who can create computer accounts, which matters for resource-based delegation.
- Rights on directory objects decide who can reset a password, add a member, write attributes or change permissions. The dangerous ones are generic-write, write-DACL, write-owner, all-extended-rights, and the right to add members to a group. Rights on a group also flow through nesting.
- Read the vendor documentation on delegation and on securing privileged accounts.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Configure three services on three computers: one with unconstrained delegation, one with constrained delegation (once with protocol transition, once without) and one with resource-based delegation. Find each with the directory module (the trusted-for-delegation flag, the allowed-to-delegate-to list, the allowed-to-act-on-behalf attribute).
2. For the unconstrained host show from the host's own ticket cache which clients' tickets it holds after a client connects.
3. Extract the access control lists of `Lab-Tier0`, its members' objects, the domain root and the domain controllers' organisational unit with `dsacls` or the directory module. List every non-default right granted to a principal that is not an administrator.
4. Write the finding table: what, why it matters, control, check.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Prepare three flawed configurations on restored snapshots (an unconstrained host, a helpdesk group with a write right over a group, a machine account quota that lets any user add computers). Draw one at random and find the weakness using only directory queries. Write the control and a query that proves it afterwards.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write an audit (PowerShell) that reports every delegation, every non-default right on privileged objects held by non-administrators, the machine account quota, and privileged accounts not marked sensitive. Run it on the flawed and the fixed domain. Apply the controls from the finding table and show each check passing.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the delegation table, the permission review, the finding table with controls and checks, and the audit's before and after output. It is accepted when each finding has a control and a check that fails before and passes after.

D33.watch_for: Reading the delegation tab in the console and missing the attributes the console does not show. Fixing the object and not the group nesting that grants the right. Granting a service more delegation to make a failure go away.

D34.title: Isolated AD misconfiguration and privilege paths
objectives: Analyze isolated AD misconfiguration — in a prepared copy of the lab domain find the planted misconfigurations (a delegated right over a group, nested membership, a weak service account password policy, an unconstrained host) from enumeration alone
Map privilege paths — turn the enumeration into a graph and find every path from a low-privilege user to `Lab-Tier0`, stating for each edge the right or membership that makes it
Design defensive fix — choose for each path the edge to cut with the least collateral effect, apply it, and show by re-collecting that the path is gone

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which delegation type leaves other users' tickets on the service host? Which right on a group lets a user add themselves to it? Name two attributes the console does not show for delegation.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Privilege in a directory is a graph: edges are memberships, rights (password reset, write members, write DACL, owner), sessions (who is logged on where), delegation and trusts. An attack path is a path in that graph; a defensive path is the same path, found first. Graph tools collect this data with ordinary read access and are used by defenders to find and cut the edges.
- Cutting a path means removing the cheapest edge that does not break a legitimate task: usually a right granted too widely, a nesting that should not exist, or a session that should not happen. Verify by collecting again.
- Collection is itself an event on the controllers (many reads); do it in a window and expect it in your own telemetry.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Restore the domain to a snapshot and plant four misconfigurations that you write down in a sealed note: a helpdesk group with a write-members right on a group nested in `Lab-Tier0`, a service account with a password in the description field, an unconstrained host, a user with a write right over another user who is a member of a privileged group.
2. Collect the domain data with BloodHound Community Edition's collector (or your own queries) and load it. Find all paths from a low-privilege user to `Lab-Tier0`.
3. For each path state every edge's cause. Verify one path by performing its first step in the lab on a test group only.
4. Cut each path with the cheapest edge, collect again, and show the paths are gone.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Restore the snapshot and apply a different set of misconfigurations chosen with a die from a list you wrote earlier. Without reading the list find all paths in the data, rank them by how much each edge would cost to cut, and propose the cuts. Then compare with the list and score what you missed and why.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Turn "no path from an ordinary account to `Lab-Tier0`" into a repeatable check: collect, query for paths, fail when any exist. Run it on the planted domain (fails with the four paths) and on the fixed domain (passes). Record how long collection takes and what a path through a trust or an off-domain system would escape.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the sealed note's planted list (after the exercise), the paths with per-edge causes, the verification of one step, the cuts and the second collection, and the repeatable check's output before and after. It is accepted when every path has a cause for every edge and the check fails before and passes after.

D34.watch_for: Planting a flaw on the real domain administrators group. Fixing the path the tool drew and missing a second one it cannot see. Trusting a graph from a collection that was missing a computer.

D35.title: Identity telemetry and detection
objectives: Identify identity telemetry — list the identity events and sources on the controllers and members, enable the auditing they need, and record what is still not collected
Build suspicious-behavior hypotheses — write six hypotheses that tie an abuse behaviour to the telemetry that would show it, with the normal baseline and the reasons for false positives

Test hardening/detection — for four hypotheses generate benign lab activity that mimics the behaviour, show whether the detection fires, record false positives and show the hardening that reduces the behaviour

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what is a path in a privilege graph and what is a cut? Which edges did the collection find that you had not planted? How would you tell your own collection from someone else's in the logs?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The sources: ticket and logon events (authentication service and ticket requests, failed pre-authentication, credential validation, logon with its type and source), special-privilege events, directory-service access and change events (object read, attribute written, member added to a group), account-management events, and endpoint events from Sysmon. Most directory events need auditing configured on the objects, not only the policy.
- A detection hypothesis has the form: if this behaviour happens, then this event with these fields appears; normal activity looks like this; these benign cases look the same. Write the baseline from measurements of your own lab, not from guesses.
- Examples to build from: service tickets with the older encryption type; one account requesting tickets for many different service names in a short time; a privileged group changing membership outside a window; directory replication rights exercised by something that is not a controller; a service principal name added to a user; a tier 0 account logging on to a lower tier.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Enable the audit policies and the object auditing (directory service changes and access) needed for your six hypotheses. Verify each source produces events.
2. Record a baseline: a script produces a day's normal activity (logons, file shares, a few administrative changes) and you note the rates.
3. Write each hypothesis in plain language with the event ids, the fields and a threshold.
4. Generate benign instances of four behaviours in the lab (use a test group and test accounts) and run the queries with `Get-WinEvent` and an XPath filter. Record which fired.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Restore the lab, run the baseline script and then three behaviours drawn at random from your list of six without noting which. Run your detections blind and name what happened and when. Record the missed ones, the false positives and the time to detection.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Tune thresholds against the false positives you measured. For two hypotheses apply the hardening that removes the behaviour (for example the encryption types, a restricted right) and show the telemetry stops. Write each detection as pseudocode with the event fields so it can become a portable rule next week, and state what each detection cannot see.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the telemetry inventory with gaps, the six hypotheses with baselines, the test results with false positives, the tuning, and the pseudocode. It is accepted when each hypothesis has a measured baseline and each tested one has a result, fired or missed, with the event.

D35.watch_for: Writing thresholds before measuring a baseline. Auditing enabled in the policy but not on the objects. A detection tested only against the behaviour it was written for.

Explain privilege/trust root cause — state for each finding the trust or permission that makes it possible, in terms of the graph

D37.title: Event sources and coverage
objectives: Inventory event sources — list every log source of the lab (hosts, DNS, firewall, web, authentication, network sensors) with what it records, its format, its retention and who can write to or delete it
Evaluate coverage gaps — map twelve behaviours from weeks 3 to 6 to the sources that could show them and mark each as no source, a weak source or a good one, with the reason
Design telemetry mapping — for each needed behaviour name the source, the fields required, the collection method and the cost, and implement collection for the three highest-value gaps

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which six identity behaviours did you write detections for last week? For one of them name the event ids and the fields. What did your baseline measure before you set a threshold?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A detection pipeline has stages: collect, normalise, store, detect, triage, respond. A weakness in an early stage cannot be repaired later: an event that was never collected cannot be detected, an event whose clock is wrong cannot be correlated.
- A coverage map relates behaviours to the telemetry that would show them. Since release v18 (October 2025) the public knowledge base of adversary techniques describes detection through detection strategies, which point to analytics for each platform, which name the log sources and data components they need; the older data sources were deprecated, so a map made before v18 uses the old vocabulary. Either is a vocabulary for the map. Coverage is not efficacy: a source that exists but is not collected, or is collected without the field you need, covers nothing.
- Logs are evidence and a target. Ask who can write to a log, who can delete it, where it is stored while it is in transit and how long it lives. Logs also hold personal data; collect what the detection needs.
- Read the data-source pages of the ATT&CK knowledge base for three techniques you met in weeks 5 and 6.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Build the inventory as a table: source, host, what it records, format, how collected today, retention, writers and deleters.
2. Choose twelve behaviours you have performed in the lab (for example account created, scheduled task created, service installed, privileged group changed, a new listening port, a web request with an injection pattern, a name lookup for an unusual domain). For each name the best source and the fields it must carry.
3. Mark gaps. Rank them by the value of the behaviour (what it would let an adversary do) and the cost of the source (volume, effort, privacy).
4. Implement collection for the top three gaps with a forwarder of your choice, send the events to the collector, and show for a benign trigger of each behaviour that the event arrives with the right host name and a correct time.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Given a short description of a small company (ten servers, a web application, a directory, a cloud mailbox, a budget of fifty gigabytes of logs a day) write a telemetry plan and a coverage matrix. Argue for what you leave out. Review your plan against the behaviours of week 12's capstone and mark which it would miss.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write telemetry unit tests: for each behaviour in your matrix a small script creates a benign trigger and then waits for the event at the collector, failing with a clear message if it does not appear within a limit. Run the suite, then disable one source and show the matching test fails. State how often the suite should run and what a pass does not prove.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the inventory, the matrix with the gap ranking, the three collection implementations with the proof of arrival (event, host, time), the test suite output with and without the disabled source, and the plan for the imaginary company. It is accepted when each cell of the matrix names a source and a field or says "no source", and each test fails when its source is disabled.

D37.watch_for: Mapping a behaviour to a source that exists but is not collected. A forwarder that sends events with the collector's clock. Reading "covered" from a matrix instead of from a test.

D38.title: Normalization and enrichment
objectives: Normalize log events — convert three different sources (Windows events, authentication and system logs, web or network logs) into one schema with named fields, types and timestamps in UTC

Validate time/source identities — verify timestamp parsing and clock skew, the resolution of host and user identities (names, security identifiers, aliases, addresses that change) and find events whose source cannot be trusted
Assess enrichment — add enrichment (asset role, user tier, network zone, indicator lists) and measure its cost, correctness and failure modes

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name three controls on a log source's integrity. What does a coverage map not tell you? Why must a telemetry test generate its own trigger?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Detection logic is written against fields. If the same fact has three names across sources (`user`, `TargetUserName`, `acct`), every rule must know all three; a common schema removes that. Public schemas exist (the Elastic Common Schema, the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework); use one as your dictionary instead of inventing names.
- Time is the first thing that goes wrong: event time against ingest time, time zones, clock skew between hosts, missing zones in the original text. Store UTC with the original text kept, and carry the skew you measured.
- Identity is the second: a user may be a name, a domain-qualified name, a security identifier or a principal name; a host a short name, a fully qualified name or an address that changed with a lease. Resolve with a time-bounded mapping and say how a failed lookup is recorded.
- Enrichment adds context (which role a host has, which tier an account belongs to) and adds failure modes: stale data, wrong joins, lookups that slow the pipeline, personal data copied into new places.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write the field dictionary for the schema you chose, limited to the fields your rules will need.
2. Write a normalizer in Python for three sources: Windows events (exported), authentication and system logs from the Linux guest, and web or Zeek logs. Emit JSON lines with typed fields, UTC time, the original time text and a source tag. Reuse your parser rules from week 1.
3. Test it with fixtures: valid events, a missing field, a time zone you did not expect, a duplicated event, an out-of-order batch.
4. Measure the clock skew of each guest against the collector and record it.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Add a fourth source (DNS or firewall logs) and a set of chaos fixtures: wrong time zone, the same event twice, half-written lines, a user in three spellings, a host renamed during the run. For each, state what the pipeline should do and what it does. Measure how many events each defect loses or mislabels.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Add data-quality monitors: events per minute for each source, the share of events missing a required field, the distribution of skew, and a heartbeat that alerts when a source goes quiet. Stop a source and move a guest's clock by ten minutes and show the monitors alert; show they are silent otherwise. State what a monitor cannot see: a source that is complete but wrong.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the dictionary, the normalizer and its tests, the skew measurements, the chaos results, the enrichment costs and the monitor output. It is accepted when every dictionary field has a test and every chaos defect has a recorded outcome.

D38.watch_for: Parsing a time with no zone as UTC. Joining on a short host name that two hosts share. Enrichment that silently turns a failed lookup into "internal".

D39.title: Sigma rules, hypotheses and fixtures
objectives: Understand Sigma schema — read and write rules in the Sigma format (log source, selections, conditions, modifiers, fields, false positives, level, tags) and explain how a rule is converted for a search system
Draft detection hypothesis — write a hypothesis (behaviour, data, expected normal activity) for a technique from week 5 or 6 and turn it into a rule
Test positive/negative fixtures — build events that must match and events that must not, run the rule through a backend and a reference evaluator you wrote, and show that both agree

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name the stages of the detection pipeline in order. What are the two ways a time field goes wrong? Which enrichment in your pipeline can fail silently?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A Sigma rule is a portable description of a detection: where the events come from, what a match looks like (selections over fields with modifiers such as contains, starts with, regular expression, address range), how the selections combine, and metadata (level, false positives, tags). A converter turns the rule into a query for a particular system through a mapping of field names and a pipeline of transformations.
- Conversion can change meaning: case sensitivity, how wildcards and escapes are handled, regular-expression dialects, field name mappings, how a missing field is treated. A rule that passes in one system and silently differs in another is a fidelity failure; the only protection is a test that runs the converted query.
- A hypothesis comes first: what behaviour, which event shows it, what normal looks like. The rule is the hypothesis in the rule format; the fixtures are its tests.
- Read the specification and the field-mapping documentation of the converter library.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Take three of last week's pseudocode detections and the three persistence checks of week 5 and write them as rules, each with a stated hypothesis.
2. Write fixtures: for each rule at least four events that must match (including variants in case and spacing) and six that must not (near misses and ordinary activity).
3. Convert each rule with the backend for your store and run the query over the fixtures. Separately write a small Python evaluator for the subset of the format you used and run the rules through it.
4. Compare the two result sets. Every disagreement is a finding: decide whether the rule, the conversion or the evaluator is wrong, and fix it.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose five rules at random from the public rule repository and convert them with your pipeline. For each decide what its data requirement is, whether your lab can satisfy it, and whether the conversion kept its meaning on your fixtures. Write at least two fixtures per rule and record any rule whose conversion differs from your evaluator.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Make one command (`make detect-test`) that runs every rule's fixtures through the backend and the evaluator and fails on any mismatch. Add a mutation test: change a modifier in one rule (for example contains to starts with) and show the suite fails. List the kinds of change the suite would not catch.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the hypotheses, the rules, the fixtures, the conversion outputs, the evaluator, the comparison with its findings, and the suite output including the mutation. It is accepted when every rule has both kinds of fixture, backend and evaluator agree on all of them, and the mutation is caught.

D39.watch_for: Writing the rule from the fixture you hold. Trusting a conversion because it ran without errors. Fixtures that only contain the exact string in the rule.

D40.title: Correlation and investigation timelines
objectives: Correlate sources — join events across sources by host, user, session and time window, handling identity and clock differences, and say what each join proves
Reconstruct investigation timeline — build a timeline of a scripted scenario in your lab from multi-source logs, with each entry tied to its event and source
Separate fact from inference — mark each statement of the timeline as observed, inferred or assumed, give its evidence and say what would change it

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what is a fixture of the negative kind and why does a rule need one? Name three ways a conversion can change a rule's meaning. What does a mutation test show?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Correlation links events that belong together. The strongest links are identifiers that the systems share (a logon session identifier that appears in the logon event and the process-creation event, the audit user id and session in the Linux audit records, the connection identifier that ties the network sensor's connection, name lookup and web records). Weaker links are time and place, which need a window and a measured skew.
- A timeline is a hypothesis with evidence. Every entry carries its source event; every statement is labelled as observed (an event shows it), inferred (a chain of reasoning from events) or assumed (no event, taken for granted). Confidence language should be consistent and should say what would raise or lower it.
- Competing explanations stay on the page until evidence removes them; a table of hypotheses against evidence (consistent, inconsistent, not informative) keeps the work honest.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write a scenario script that a clone runs while you do not watch: a user logs on, creates a scheduled task, looks up an unusual name, downloads a file from the lab web server, installs a service. Everything is benign and writes a marker.
2. Collect all sources for the period. Normalise them with last week's tool.
3. Build the timeline: join the logon to the process start by session identifier, the process to the network connection, the name lookup to the connection. Note every join's key and its weakness.
4. Label each statement observed, inferred or assumed with the evidence, and list what you would ask the owner of each system.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Run a second scenario drawn at random from three you prepared and describe within ninety minutes what happened, from the logs only. Write the competing hypotheses and the evidence against each. Then read the script and mark where you went beyond the evidence and what you missed.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Express one correlation as a detection: the sequence of a logon, a scheduled task creation and a lookup of a name not seen in the baseline within ten minutes. Implement it as a correlation rule or as code over your normalised store. Test it with the scenario, with three benign variants (each missing one step or exceeding the window) and with the baseline's ordinary activity, and record the false positives.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the scenario script, the timeline with sources and keys, the labels with evidence, the hypothesis table, the questions for owners, and the sequence detection with its tests. It is accepted when every timeline entry cites an event and no statement lacks a label.

D40.watch_for: Joining on time alone when an identifier exists. A timeline entry with no event behind it. Writing "the attacker" where the evidence says "a process".

D41.title: Detection criteria and false-positive estimation
objectives: Define detection criteria — state for a rule what it must detect, the data it needs, its severity, the response it triggers and its acceptance criteria (the fixtures it must match and a false-positive budget per day)
Estimate false positives — measure a rule against a baseline of normal activity, estimate its false-positive rate with an interval, and say what the estimate does not cover
Refine rule — refine the rule to meet its budget without losing the fixtures it must catch, and record the trade-off of each change

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the join keys you used yesterday and how each could break. Write one sentence for each of observed, inferred and assumed. Why does the sequence detection need benign variants?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A detection is a classifier: it has precision (how many alerts are real) and recall (how much of the real activity it catches). When real events are rare, even a low false-positive rate buries them: a rule that fires wrongly on one event in a hundred, on a source that produces a hundred thousand events a day, produces a thousand false alerts a day. Budget the false positives first.
- Estimate rates from counts over a stated period with an interval, not from a single day's number. If no false positive was observed in N independent trials, the upper bound at about ninety-five percent confidence is roughly three divided by N.
- Tuning by exclusion removes alerts and creates blind spots; record each exclusion with its reason and the evasion it permits. Keep fixtures for the evasions you know (a renamed binary, different case, encoded arguments) and track which ones the rule misses.
- A rule has a lifecycle: hypothesis, rule, tests, deployment, monitoring, retirement. Its severity and response must be decided before it fires.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Build a baseline: generate three days of ordinary lab activity (a generator that logs users in, runs jobs, browses, patches) plus the noise of your guests.
2. Write acceptance criteria for three rules: the fixtures to match, the data required, the severity, the response and the budget.
3. Run each rule over the baseline and count alerts. Classify them as true, false or unknown. Estimate the false-positive rate per day with an interval.
4. Refine each rule to meet its budget. After every change rerun the fixtures; record the trade-off.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Choose three public rules at random, convert them and measure them against your baseline. For each decide whether it is deployable under your budget, refine it, and record the exclusions with their blind spots. Write three evasion fixtures per rule and record which the refined rule misses.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Automate the acceptance: a test that fails if any must-match fixture is missed, if the false-positive upper bound on the baseline exceeds the budget, or if a known evasion that previously matched stops matching. Run it before and after a deliberate change that over-tunes a rule, and show it fails. List what the baseline does not represent (a different season, a new application).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the criteria, the baseline description, the counts and intervals, the refinements and their trade-offs, the evasion table and the acceptance test output. It is accepted when every rule has a measured rate with an interval and every exclusion names the evasion it permits.

D41.watch_for: A rate from one quiet day. Excluding a process name that an adversary can also choose. A budget set after seeing the alerts.
