D42.title: Week 7 assessment (blind practical)
objectives: Investigate blind telemetry — investigate an unseen set of multi-source telemetry from a stated hypothesis and reconstruct what happened
Implement evidence-based detection — write two rules for behaviours you found, with positive and negative fixtures and a false-positive estimate
Report limitations — state what the telemetry could not show, which conclusions are observed, inferred or assumed, and what would change them

sections.name: Blind practical
sections.markdown: Open the assessment in the application, start the attempt and read the task statement. Take the telemetry from the source you fixed before the week and do not read its description before the clock starts. Stop at 120 minutes.

sections.name: Remediation
sections.markdown: Grade yourself against the rubric before reading any answer key. For every criterion below your target find the cause in your method (a source you did not query, a join you did not verify, a rule with no negative fixture) and fix it with a short exercise on your own data. Then redo the failed part on different telemetry.

sections.name: Report
sections.markdown: Write the report in the structure of the task statement: hypothesis, timeline with labels, findings, the two rules with fixtures and estimates, limitations. Attach the evidence with SHA-256 values.

sections.name: Performance review
sections.markdown: Compare the grade with the week's targets: independent execution, a stated hypothesis before searching, every statement labelled, detections with negative fixtures and a measured rate, honest limits. Record the three habits that cost you most and one change for next week.

D42.watch_for: Searching before stating a hypothesis. A rule with no negative fixture. Calling an inference an observation.

D43.title: Incident scoping, severity and evidence preservation
objectives: Scope incident and severity — from an initial report define what is affected, what is known and unknown, a severity with stated criteria, and the first questions and decisions
Preserve evidence — collect and preserve volatile and non-volatile evidence from a lab host in a defensible order, with hashes and a custody record, changing what you collect as little as you can
Draft triage plan — write a plan with priorities, owners, time boxes, containment options and their risks, and the decision points

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which two hunts did you run last week and what did each find? What does a null result tell the reader that "nothing found" does not? Name three limits of the false-positive estimate you made.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Incident handling is a cycle: prepare, detect and analyse, contain and eradicate and recover, then learn. The national standard for incident handling (NIST SP 800-61) describes the activities and, in its current revision, aligns them to the cybersecurity framework's functions. Read it for vocabulary; the plan is yours.
- Scoping asks: what is the report, what systems and data are involved, what is the business effect, what is known, what is assumed, who decides containment, who must be told and by when. Severity needs criteria written before the incident (impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability, scope, data class, time criticality); the number is a decision aid, not a fact.
- Evidence is collected in order of volatility (RFC 3227): processor state and memory first, then network state and running processes, then disk, then remote logs. Every action changes the system; record what you did, when, with what tool and its version, and hash everything you keep. Work on copies, keep originals read-only, and say what you did not collect.
- A custody record says who held what, when, where and what they did with it, so that a stranger can believe the evidence is what you say it is.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Run a scenario on two clones (one Linux, one Windows) that a helper prepared: a user reports unexpected behaviour. Write the scoping questions you would ask, the answers you have, and the assumptions you are making. Choose a severity with criteria.
2. Collect from the Linux clone: running processes, sockets, logged-on users and the time with its source; then a memory image through the hypervisor, then a copy of the disk image. From the Windows clone: a memory dump through the hypervisor, then the disk image. Hash every item at once and again after copying.
3. Keep a custody record as you work (what, when in UTC, who, how, hash).
4. Write the triage plan: first hour, first day, containment options with risks (isolate, snapshot, stop, rebuild), decision points and who decides.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: A second scenario is prepared on a different clone from a list you wrote. Without reading the list, within sixty minutes write the scoping record, severity and plan, and within the rest of the block preserve the evidence with a custody record. Then list every assumption you made and what would have disproved it.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Build an evidence intake tool: it hashes a file, stores it read-only, and appends a record (what, when, who, hash, previous record's hash) to a custody log whose entries link to each other. A second command verifies the whole log and every stored file. Tamper with a stored file and with a log entry and show the verification finds both; state what the log cannot prove (that the evidence was genuine before you took it).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the scoping record, the severity criteria and result, the custody log with its verification output, the hash list, and the plan. It is accepted when every preserved item has a hash taken at collection and verified after copying, and every assumption is written down.

D43.watch_for: Rebooting the clone before taking memory. Hashing after copying only. A severity chosen before the scoping questions were answered.

D44.title: Host artifacts and the event timeline
objectives: Analyze host artifacts — extract and interpret key artifacts from Windows and Linux images (evidence of execution, persistence, account activity, file system timestamps, logs) with a tool and by hand

Construct event timeline — merge artifacts into one timeline in UTC, normalise timestamps with their exact semantics (modified, accessed, changed, created) and mark what each source can and cannot prove
Explain chain-of-custody assumptions — state what each conclusion assumes about the integrity of the evidence (acquisition method, tool, clock, hash) and what would invalidate it

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the order of volatility from most to least volatile. Write the fields of a custody record. What is the difference between a severity and a priority?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Artifacts are by-products of use: on Windows the execution records (prefetch files, application compatibility and amcache entries), registry hives, shell and jump-list records, the master file table and the change journal, event logs; on Linux the authentication and system logs, the login records, shell history, scheduled jobs, package manager logs, file timestamps, `~/.ssh`. Each records something different and is kept for a different time.
- File timestamps have meanings that depend on the file system and mount options. Modified and changed are not created; access times may not be updated at all; a copy keeps or resets times depending on the tool. Some systems store two sets of times for the same file; differences between them are a clue to time manipulation, not proof of it.
- A timeline merges sources into one clock. Normalise to UTC, keep the original text, note each source's resolution and its known skew, and do not conclude from one source what another could contradict.
- Read the documentation of the timeline and file system tools you use, and the sections of SP 800-86 on data collection and examination.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Mount the images read-only with the access times left alone. Record the command that makes the mount read-only and show that a write is refused.
2. On the Linux image extract logs, history, scheduled jobs, `~/.ssh`, package logs and the listing of recently changed files. On the Windows image extract execution evidence, the registry hives, event logs and the file system metadata with the tools of your choice.
3. Build a super-timeline with Plaso for each image, filter it to the scenario's window, and verify five entries by reading the artifact itself.
4. For three timestamps explain exactly what the time means (which attribute, which file system, which tool) and what would make it wrong.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Restore a second prepared image pair and build the timeline within ninety minutes. Mark each entry's source and resolution, flag every place where two sources disagree and say which you trust and why. Then read the helper's script and mark what your timeline missed and what it invented.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Assess forensic readiness: list which artifacts your lab would no longer hold ninety days from now (log rotation, disabled history, solid-state trim, short event log sizes) and what each loss would cost an investigator. Implement three improvements (longer retention, command-line auditing, forwarding to the collector), then rerun the scenario and show the evidence of the improved items.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the extracted artifacts with their sources, the merged timeline with resolution and skew notes, the verified entries, the three timestamp explanations, the assumptions list and the readiness changes with their proof. It is accepted when every timeline entry names its artifact and every conclusion lists what it assumes.

D44.watch_for: Mounting read-write and changing the evidence. Treating a file's modified time as the time of an action. A timeline in local time with no zone.

D45.title: Network evidence
objectives: Analyze suspicious PCAP — read a capture for a suspicious conversation (a regular beacon, an odd name lookup, a large upload, an unusual protocol use) and describe it with flows and statistics
Correlate network and host evidence — tie flows to host processes and users using time, ports and host logs, and state the strength of each link
Identify gaps — state what the capture cannot show (encryption, sampling, missing segments, address translation) and what other evidence would close each gap

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name the artifact that shows a program ran and one that shows only that it existed. What does the modified time of a file tell you and what does it not? Where do you record the clock error of an image?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A capture is a set of packets; a flow log (as Zeek writes) is a summary of conversations. Start from the summary: who talked to whom, how much, how often, for how long. Then read the packets that matter.
- Suspicious patterns are statistical before they are specific: connections at near-regular intervals (a beacon, with or without random delay), a few very large outbound transfers, names that look generated, a protocol on an unexpected port, a certificate that does not match its name. Each has benign look-alikes (software updates, time synchronisation, monitoring checks).
- Encrypted traffic still carries metadata: addresses, sizes, timing, the server name in the handshake, certificate fields. It does not carry content; say so.
- A flow becomes evidence about a host only when it is tied to the host: by the address and port at the time, by the host's own records of the connection, by the process that owned the socket. The link has a strength; write it down.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Take the capture of the scenario's network from the router and run Zeek over it. Read the connection, name lookup, web and certificate logs. Use Wireshark's conversation and endpoint statistics and the I/O graph.
2. Compute inter-arrival times for each destination with a short Python script and find the one with the most regular intervals. Check the lookups preceding it.
3. Tie the flow to a host process using the Windows guest's connection events and the Linux guest's socket snapshot taken at the time. State the link's strength (time-only, address and port, process-owned).
4. List what you could not see and what would close each gap.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Analyse a capture you have not seen: choose one from a public source of training captures, or a scenario recorded by a helper. Examine flows only: do not extract files from captures of real malware. Describe the three most suspicious conversations with their statistics and the benign explanations you excluded.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write a beacon detector over the connection logs: group by source and destination, compute the regularity of intervals (for example the spread relative to the mean) and alert on regular, long-lived patterns. Test it with a synthetic beacon with and without random delay, with periodic benign traffic (time synchronisation, updates) as false-positive tests, and record the thresholds. State what an adversary can do to hide from it.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the flow statistics, the three conversations with reasoning, the host links with their strength, the detector with its test results and the gap list. It is accepted when every link is labelled with its strength and every gap names the evidence that would close it.

D45.watch_for: Taking a regular interval as proof: updates are regular too. Linking a flow to a process by time alone. Opening files carried in a capture of real malware.

D46.title: Static triage of a safe malware fixture
objectives: Inspect safe static malware fixture — examine a benign fixture built to look suspicious without running it (type, hashes, strings, headers, imports, sections, entropy, embedded data, signing)
Record static characteristics — record every characteristic with the command, tool version and output, in a form another analyst can reproduce

Distinguish behavior from static inference — separate what the file can be observed to contain from what you infer it would do, label each, and say what a dynamic analysis would add and what it would risk

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what makes a network link between a flow and a process strong or weak? Name two benign things that beacon. What does an encrypted flow still reveal?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Static analysis examines a file without running it. It is safe by construction and limited by construction: it shows what is present (strings, imports, structure, embedded data), not what happens. Packing, encryption and obfuscation hide content from static views and are themselves evidence, usually of intent to hide.
- Identify with hashes (use SHA-256; short hashes collide), file type by content and not by name, headers and sections, the functions the file imports, readable strings, embedded resources and the entropy of each section (a very high value suggests compressed or encrypted data). Tools such as `capa` describe capabilities that follow from the imports and code patterns; they are inferences.
- A detection rule for a file (YARA) names byte patterns and conditions. It must be specific enough not to match benign programs and tested against a corpus of them.
- Handling rules: never execute an unknown program on a host you care about; keep samples renamed and in an archive with a clear marker; do not run anything even in the lab without a written decision for that sample.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Build three benign fixtures yourself: a small compiled program that references network functions and carries an embedded address and an encoded string but only prints a message; a program with a large high-entropy data section; a script with encoded-looking but harmless strings. Do not run them.
2. Triage one of them (chosen by your helper) as if it were unknown: file type, SHA-256, strings, headers and sections, imports, entropy, embedded data, any signature. Record each command with its tool version and the output.
3. Run `capa` and read what it infers and from what. Write what you would expect the file to do, separately from what you observed it contains.
4. Write a YARA rule that identifies the fixture by two or more independent features.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Have a helper or a script prepare three fixtures, one of them a decoy that looks suspicious and is plain, and give you one without saying which. Triage it blind in ninety minutes and write the report with a confidence for each statement. Then compare with what the fixture was built to do and record which inferences were wrong and why.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Test your rule for false positives against a corpus of benign programs (the system binaries of your guests and a set of open source programs) and record any match. Tighten the rule until it has none while still matching the fixture and a recompiled variant of it. Record the variants it misses (a different compiler setting, a changed string) and say what that means for how long the rule would stay useful.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the triage record with commands and tool versions, the inferred behaviour with confidence labels, the rule, the false-positive test and the list of variants it misses. It is accepted when each characteristic is reproducible from its recorded command and each behavioural statement is labelled observed, inferred or assumed.

D46.watch_for: Running the fixture "just to see". Reading a capability list as a behaviour. A rule built on one string.

D47.title: Hypothesis-driven hunting
objectives: Define hunt hypothesis — write a hunt hypothesis from a threat behaviour, an intelligence report or a gap in your coverage, with the data it needs, the normal pattern expected and the criteria for stopping
Examine approved telemetry — run the hunt over the approved telemetry (your store and datasets) and record the queries, the volume examined and what you excluded and why
Record findings/detections — document the findings (including none), the confidence, and convert any repeatable finding into a rule with fixtures

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list five static characteristics you recorded yesterday and the command for each. Which of your statements were inferred? What would a dynamic analysis have added and what would it have risked?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A hunt looks for activity that no rule has caught. It starts from a hypothesis that is specific and testable, names the data it needs, and says what normal looks like. It ends with a finding, an improvement (a new rule, a new source) or a recorded null result with the coverage it had.
- Attackers change tools more easily than behaviours. The pyramid of pain ranks what you can detect by how costly it is to change: hash values, addresses, domain names, artifacts, tools, techniques. Hunt higher up when you can.
- Hunt only in telemetry you are approved to examine. Write the approval and the scope in the report; do not widen the data because it would be interesting. Personal data seen during a hunt is handled as the policy says.
- A null result is a result: it says the behaviour was not seen in this data over this period, with these exclusions, and nothing about data you did not examine.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write two hypotheses: a scheduled task or service created from a parent process that is not an administrative tool; outbound connections from servers to destinations seen rarely, at near-regular intervals.
2. For each state the data, the normal pattern, the stopping criteria. Run them over the lab store and one dataset you chose, recording each query, the number of events examined and the time range.
3. Classify what you find as true, benign or unknown, and what you excluded and why. Record the confidence.
4. Convert the first hypothesis into a rule with positive and negative fixtures and run it over the baseline.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Take one technique at random from the knowledge base's list and write and run a hunt for it over your data. Document either a finding or a null result. State the share of hosts and time your data covered, so that a null result can be read correctly.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Make the hunt repeatable: store the queries as code with parameters, run them against a snapshot of the store, and produce the report skeleton automatically. Measure what the first hunt's rule alerts on across the baseline and record its false positives. Add the hunt to a schedule and note what review the output needs.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the hypotheses, queries, volumes, exclusions, findings and confidence, the converted rule with its fixtures and false-positive measurement, and the repeatable hunt code. It is accepted when each hunt names its approved data, its coverage and its stopping criteria.

D47.watch_for: A hypothesis too vague to fail. Widening the data when the first query finds nothing. Reporting a null result as "clean".

D49.title: Mapping an LLM application and its threat model
objectives: Map LLM application — draw the components of the application (front end, orchestration, system prompt, retrieval, model, tools, memory, logs) and the data that flows between them, from the code and the running system

Identify data/tool boundaries — mark who can write each input (users, document authors, tool providers), which inputs reach the model, which outputs reach tools or other users, and what authority each tool carries
Threat-model application — enumerate threats for the model, the retrieval path, the tools and the logs, rank them with evidence, and write each as a testable security requirement

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which controls of week 8 would you apply before touching a memory image? Name the two kinds of evidence a timeline mixes. What did your hunts report as their coverage?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- An LLM application is a pipeline around a model: input from a user, a system prompt from the developer, context retrieved from stores, tool definitions and tool results, and the model's output, which is shown to a user or passed to code. The model sees all of it as one stream of text. That is the root of prompt injection: data and instructions share a channel.
- The model is not a security boundary and cannot enforce an authorization rule. Authorization, isolation and validation belong in code before the model (what it may see) and after it (what its output may do). Assume the system prompt can be disclosed and put no secret in it.
- A threat model of such an application asks the usual questions of each element (who can write this, who can read it, what can it cause) and adds: what happens if the model follows an instruction that was inside data; what happens if its output is wrong, malformed or hostile; what happens if two users share a cache, a memory or an index.
- Read the project's list of the most serious risks for applications built on language models (the current edition) and the national taxonomy of attacks on machine learning systems for vocabulary.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Build version 0 of the application: a question-answering tool over a synthetic corpus for three tenants and three roles, with retrieval by similarity, a system prompt, and three tools (search documents, create a ticket in a sandbox, send a message to a sandbox address). Keep it small enough to read in an hour.
2. From the code and by running it, list every route by which text reaches the model and every route by which model output reaches a person, a tool or a store.
3. Draw the data-flow diagram with trust boundaries and mark the assets (system prompt, restricted documents, tool credentials, logs).
4. Write threats for each element and boundary, rank them, and write twelve security requirements that a test could check (for example "retrieval returns only documents the requesting user may read, decided in code before the prompt is built").

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Run a different open-source retrieval application from a public repository in your lab, offline, and map it in ninety minutes from its code and behaviour alone. Produce the diagram, the five threats you rank highest and one test that would show the most serious. Then compare your map with its documentation and note what it did not tell you.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Turn the twelve requirements into a skeleton test file: for each a test with a name, a setup and an expected outcome, most of which fail or are skipped today. Implement the three that need no model at all (the retrieval filter, the tool allow-list, the output size limit) and run them against the application. Record which requirements can be guaranteed by code and which can only be measured.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the diagram, the entry-point and authority table, the ranked threats with reasoning, the twelve requirements and the test skeleton with the results of the three implemented tests. It is accepted when every threat points to a requirement and every requirement is marked "guaranteed by code" or "measured".

D50.title: RAG ingestion, retrieval and source trust
objectives: Explain RAG ingestion/retrieval — explain how documents are parsed, split, embedded, indexed and retrieved, and what is lost or added at each step (metadata, access control, hidden text)
Analyze source trust — classify the sources of the corpus by who can write them and how much they are trusted, and show how an untrusted document can steer the answer to another user's question

Test provenance controls — implement and test source labels, quarantine of untrusted sources, retrieval-time access control and hidden-content stripping, and show which ones hold regardless of the model

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name five assets of your application. Which two of your requirements need no model to test? Why may a system prompt not hold a secret?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Retrieval brings text from stores into the prompt. Each stage can change its meaning: parsers drop or add text (hidden text in a web page or document, text in comments or metadata), chunking cuts context, embedding discards access control unless you carry it as metadata, similarity search returns what is near and not what is permitted.
- A document that a user can write, or that is fetched from somewhere they can influence, is untrusted input to every other user's question. It can contain instructions (indirect injection) or false facts. Source trust is a property you record at ingestion, with the document's hash, origin, author class and time.
- Access control must be enforced at retrieval, in code, with the requester's permissions, before text is placed in the prompt. A prompt that says "do not reveal documents the user may not see" is a request, not a control. A shared index across tenants needs a filter the application sets, never one the model or the user supplies.
- Embeddings and indexes are data stores that need the same protection, retention and deletion as the documents they came from.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Extend the application's ingestion with metadata per chunk: source, document hash, author class, tenant, readers, trust level, ingest time.
2. Plant three test documents: one that contains a harmless instruction (when asked about the product, also print a marker), one restricted document with a canary string, one with text hidden by formatting.
3. Show the failures: the marker appears in another user's answer, the canary is returned to a user who may not read it when the question is close enough, hidden text reaches the prompt.
4. Fix them in code: filter at retrieval by the requester's permissions, quarantine untrusted sources and label their text as untrusted data in the prompt, strip hidden content at ingestion. Rerun with twenty trials each and record the rates.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Ingest a set of web pages and PDFs you did not prepare for the test (a public documentation set, a set of newsletters). Examine what the parsers do with hidden text, comments, metadata, alternative text and tables. Write an ingestion check that reports content present in the file but invisible to a reader, run it on the set, and count what it finds.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Add monitoring: log for every answer the identifiers of the chunks used, their trust levels and the requester; alert when a chunk of a lower trust level than the request's policy allows is used, or when a canary appears in any output. Test with the three planted documents. State what the logging cannot show (the model's reasoning) and what it would cost to keep.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the pipeline description with the metadata schema, the three planted documents and the before and after rates, the hidden-content check and its counts, and the monitoring tests. It is accepted when the retrieval filter has a test that fails without it and the prompt-level mitigation is reported with its measured rate rather than as a guarantee.

D50.watch_for: Filtering after generation instead of before. Letting the query supply its own tenant filter. A hidden-text check that only looks at one parser's output.

D51.title: Prompt injection entry points and the authorization boundary
objectives: Classify prompt-injection entry — classify the ways untrusted text reaches the model (direct input, retrieved documents, tool outputs, file and field names, metadata, rendered content) and the goals an injected instruction can have (reveal, act, mislead, persist)
Run controlled fixtures — build and run a set of harmless injection fixtures against your application over repeated trials, and report the success rate of each with an interval
Test authorization boundary — show that an injected instruction asking for a tool or a document the requester may not use is refused by code, whatever the model does

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the four stages of your ingestion where text can change meaning. What is the difference between a filter at retrieval and a warning in the prompt? Name the trust levels you recorded.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Direct injection is the user's own text trying to override the developer's instructions; indirect injection arrives in content the application fetches on the user's behalf. The second is the serious one because the victim never typed it. Goals include disclosing context, causing an action through a tool, producing misleading output, and storing an instruction for later.
- Defences differ in kind. Statistical: instructions to the model, delimiters, filters on input and output, classifiers; they lower the rate and never reach zero, and attackers adapt. Structural: remove the capability (a tool that cannot send data out cannot exfiltrate), limit authority to the requester's own, require approval for sensitive actions, block outbound channels such as rendered links and images, isolate untrusted content from control flow.
- Because model behaviour varies between runs, a single success or failure means nothing. Repeat each fixture many times at fixed settings, report the success rate with an interval, and keep the model version and settings with the result.
- Read the project's description of the risk and at least one practitioner's account of attacks through documents and tools.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write thirty fixtures with harmless goals: print a marker, reveal a canary, call a tool with a marker argument, try to call a tool the requester cannot use, try to send retrieved text to an address. Spread them across entry points: the user's message, a retrieved document, a tool result, a file name, a field of metadata.
2. Run each twenty times at fixed settings. Record the success rate and a Wilson interval, with model, quantisation and settings.
3. For every fixture that tried to use a tool or document beyond the requester's authority, show whether the attempt was refused by code. Write the test: even with a scripted model that always makes the attempt, the call is denied.
4. Rank the fixtures by rate and by impact.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Run a scanner (`garak` or the red-team features of `promptfoo`) against your application. Triage its findings: which are true failures of the application, which are model behaviours with no impact because of structural controls, which are noise. Compare with your fixtures' results and list what each approach found that the other did not.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Apply structural defences: authority of every tool call derived from the requester (not from the model's arguments), approval required for the sensitive tool with the exact arguments shown, outbound content stripped of links and images to other origins. Rerun the thirty fixtures and show the impact-bearing ones drop to zero by construction while the statistical ones keep a measured rate. Record what the defences cost in usability.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the taxonomy, the fixtures with rates and intervals, the scripted-model authorization tests, the scanner triage and the before and after table. It is accepted when every impact-bearing fixture is stopped by a deterministic test and every rate carries its interval and settings.

D51.watch_for: Concluding "it works" from three runs. A scripted-model test that never tries the forbidden call. Counting a refusal by the model as a refusal by the application.

D52.title: Output handling, schemas and unsafe tools
objectives: Analyze output schema failures — show how malformed, extra, mistyped or hostile model output breaks code that parses or uses it, and where the output becomes input to another interpreter (SQL, shell, HTML, a URL)

Examine unsafe tools — review each tool of the application for authority, inputs, side effects and reachable resources, and find the unsafe patterns (arbitrary path or address, command construction, broad credentials, no limits)
Define typed enforcement — specify and implement validation of every model-proposed call against a schema and a policy in code before anything executes

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: write the confidence interval method you used for success rates. Which of your fixtures changed behaviour with the model's settings? Name two structural defences and what each removes.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Output from a model is untrusted input for whatever consumes it. If it is placed in a page it is a script-injection risk; if it is placed in a query, a command, a path or a URL it is an injection or request-forgery risk; if it is parsed it may be malformed. All of week 3 and week 4 applies to it.
- A tool is an authority grant: it carries credentials, can have side effects and can reach resources. The questions to ask of every tool are who it acts for, what it can touch, what happens on a wrong call, and how a wrong call is noticed.
- Typed enforcement means the model proposes and code decides: the proposed call is parsed against a schema (fields, types, ranges, lengths, allowed values), checked against policy (is this requester allowed to do this to this object), limited (rate, size, time) and recorded. Anything else is refused and the refusal is returned to the model as data.
- Dry-run modes, idempotency keys and approvals for destructive actions bound the cost of the cases that slip through.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add to the application three tools in unsafe form: a query tool that builds SQL from the model's text, a fetch tool that retrieves any address, a file tool that takes a path.
2. With harmless markers show each failure: a query that returns another tenant's row, a fetch of an internal address of your lab, a path outside the sandbox directory. Use a scripted model so the result is reproducible.
3. Replace each with a typed version: parameterised queries with an allow-list of columns, a destination allow-list with the checks of week 4, a path resolved inside the sandbox directory. Add schema validation of every call, a per-requester policy check and a size and rate limit.
4. Test every cell of the matrix with valid, boundary and hostile arguments.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Write five tool definitions that a colleague might plausibly add (read a file, run a command, fetch a web page, query a database, send an email) in their naive form. Audit each for authority, inputs, side effects and reachable resources, rank them by risk, and write the minimal safe form and the test that would catch the naive one.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Fuzz the validation layer with hostile arguments (very long values, nested structures, type confusion, path and address tricks, encodings) generated by a script, and show every invalid call is refused with a recorded reason and no side effect. Add the approval path for the one destructive tool and test replay of an approval with changed arguments. State what the validation cannot know (whether a valid call is a wise one).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the matrix with a test name for each cell, the naive and safe versions with their results, the fuzzing summary and the approval tests. It is accepted when no invalid call reaches a side effect and each cell is backed by a test that fails on the naive tool.

D52.watch_for: Validating the shape and not the meaning of an argument. A tool that runs with the application's own credentials when the requester has fewer. An error message that returns internal detail to the model.

D53.title: Independent evaluation design
objectives: Design independent eval cases — write evaluation cases that were not used to build the defences, partition them into development and held-out sets, and state the scoring rule for each before running

Separate model from app security — test the application's guarantees with an adversarial model stub so that they are shown to hold whatever the model does, and measure the real model's behaviour separately
Report actual limitations — report the results with their intervals, the settings and versions, and what the evaluation cannot show, including the risk that the test data leaked into your tuning

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: for each of your tools name the three questions to ask of it. What does a typed boundary do with a refused call? Name a defence that cannot be shown by a unit test.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Two different claims need two different tests. "The application never returns a document the requester may not read" is a guarantee: test it with a stub that behaves as badly as an attacker could, and expect no failures. "The model usually refuses an injected instruction" is a statistic: repeat, report the rate with an interval, and keep the version and settings.
- Independent means the test cases were not used to build or tune the defences. Write them after the application is frozen, keep a held-out set you do not run until the end, and record what you changed after seeing results. Looking at the test set while tuning leaks it.
- Scoring rules are decided before the run. A model used as a judge is another model whose errors and biases must be measured against labels you made by hand.
- Report: system and model versions and hashes, settings, number of trials, intervals, failures with examples, and the limits of the data and of the cases.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Freeze version 1 of the application (all week's defences in). Write sixty new cases across entry points, goals and roles, with an expected outcome and a scoring rule for each. Split into a development set of thirty and a held-out set of thirty.
2. Build an adversarial model stub that always attempts the attack in each case. Run the stub against the whole set: every guarantee test must pass.
3. Run the real model twenty times on the development set. Compute rates and intervals. Fix anything you decide to fix, and write down each change.
4. Run the held-out set once. Report the rates and compare with the development results.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Take an evaluation someone else published (a benchmark description or a vendor's safety claim) and critique its validity in one page: what it measures, how the cases were made, the number of trials, nondeterminism, prompt sensitivity, leakage of test data, and what the reported number does not show. Redo one of its measurements on your application if you can.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Make the evaluation a gate: a command that runs the guarantee tests with the stub (must be all green) and the statistical tests with a threshold on the upper bound of the failure rate, stores each run with model hash, settings and date, and fails the change if a rate worsens beyond its interval. Introduce a regression (loosen the retrieval filter) and show the gate stops it.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the protocol, the cases and the scoring rules, the stub results, the intervals for the real model, the held-out comparison, the critique and the gate's output with and without the regression. It is accepted when the guarantee tests and the statistical tests are reported separately and the held-out set was run once.

D55.title: Agent workflow and authority crossings
objectives: Map agent workflow — draw the loop of the agent (plan, propose a call, validate, execute, observe, decide) as a state machine with the data and the identity at each step

Identify authority crossings — mark every point where authority moves (user to agent, agent to tool, tool to an external system, a tool result back into the model, a memory write) and say what constrains each
Define bounded execution — specify and enforce limits on steps, time, tokens, spend, tools and side effects, with a way to stop the agent that does not depend on the model

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: which two of last week's measures are guarantees and which are statistics? Name the property that makes an evaluation independent. What did your adversarial stub prove that the real model could not?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- An agent turns a model's text into actions. Its security depends less on the model than on the loop around it: which tools exist, with whose credentials they run, what is checked before a call, what limits apply, and what happens to results.
- Authority crossings are where defects live: a user's request delegates some of the user's authority to the agent; a tool exercises an authority that may be larger than the user's (a service account); a tool result carries untrusted text back into the model; a memory write stores a decision for later; a tool that fetches content gives an outsider a way to speak to the agent.
- Excess comes in three kinds: more functionality than the task needs, more permission than the functionality needs, and more autonomy than the consequences allow. Bounded execution addresses all three: a short tool list, narrow credentials, step and time limits, approval for consequential steps, and a stop that code controls.
- Read the agentic threat guidance of the application security community and the protocol-independent parts of the model context specification on tools and consent.

sections.markdown:
1. Build the agent: a loop in which the model proposes a tool call as structured data, code validates and executes it in the sandbox, and the result is returned as data. Give it four tools: read a file in the scratch directory, fetch a page through an allow-listed proxy, write a note, run a snippet in the sandbox without network.
2. Draw the loop as a state machine. Mark each crossing with its authority, the check applied and the data that crosses.
3. Implement the limits: maximum steps, wall-clock time, tokens, number of calls per tool, output size, and an allow-list of tools per task. Add a stop that an operator can trigger from outside the process.
4. Write the tests with the adversarial stub: a model that loops forever, one that calls a tool not on the list, one that asks for ten thousand files, one that ignores the stop. Each must be contained.

Remove one limit and show the matching test fails. State which consequences the limits cannot bound (a single valid but harmful call).

D56.title: Identities, scopes and excessive agency
objectives: Examine identities/scopes — list the identities in the system (user, agent, each tool backend) and the credentials and scopes each tool call carries, and compare them with the minimum the task needs
Identify excessive agency — find the tools that have more functionality, permission or autonomy than their task needs, and show the harm a wrong call could do with each

Design backend approvals — design and implement approval for consequential actions in the backend, bound to the exact operation, resource and requester, single use and expiring, and test it against replay and tampering

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the six limits you put on the agent. Which of them stops a loop inside a tool? Why must a kill switch not rely on the model?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Whose authority does a call carry? Three answers exist and only one is safe by default: the agent's own broad service credential (the agent can do anything the credential can, for anyone who asks), a credential delegated from the user for this task and these objects (the call can do what the user could), or none (the tool is only a proposal). Prefer delegated, narrow, short-lived credentials.
- Excessive agency has three parts: tools with more functionality than needed (a tool that can delete when the task is to read), with more permission than their function needs (a database role that can write everywhere), and with more autonomy than the consequences allow (sending, paying, deleting without a person).
- Approval is a control only if the approver sees what will happen and the approval binds to exactly that: the operation, the resource, the parameters, the requester, an expiry and a single use, verified by the backend when the call is made and not by the agent. The approval prompt must be produced by trusted code from the stored request, never from text the model wrote.
- The approval design of this program's application is a worked example: a request records the operation hash, the resource and its revision; the grant is made through a confirmation the application itself shows; the grant is consumed once; a message authentication code binds it.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. List the identities and for each tool the credential it runs with and the scopes that credential holds. Compare with the minimum each task needs and mark the excess.
2. Add a destructive tool (delete a ticket in the sandbox service) and a sending tool. Demonstrate with a scripted model the harm of an over-broad credential: the agent deletes a ticket the requester does not own.
3. Replace ambient credentials with delegated tokens: the backend issues a token per task bound to the requester, the objects and the scopes. Show the same scripted model's call is now refused.
4. Implement the approval: the agent proposes, the backend stores the request with the exact parameters, a person approves through a separate channel that displays the stored request, the backend verifies and consumes the approval when the call arrives. Test replay, changed parameters, a different resource, an expired approval and an approval of someone else's request.

sections.markdown: Review a design in which an agent runs tools with credentials taken from environment variables of the tool process. Write the findings, refactor the design to scoped delegated tokens on paper and in code for one tool, and prove with a test that a token for one task cannot be used for another.

sections.name: Defence and verification

D57.title: MCP transport, actors and tokens
objectives: Analyze MCP transport and actors — identify the host, client, servers, authorization server and resource server in a working setup, the transport each uses, and what each trusts

Examine token audience and exfil risk — show how a token for one server presented to another is or is not accepted, how a tool description or result can carry instructions, and how a tool with a destination argument can move data out
Define MCP regression cases — write tests that fail on the vulnerable server and pass on the fixed one for audience, expiry, tool-definition change, destination arguments and path arguments

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: draw the approval protocol and mark what is bound. Which three kinds of excess does a tool have? What does a scope audit based on usage miss?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The protocol connects a host application, which runs one client per server, to servers that offer tools, resources and prompts over a transport (a local process over standard streams, or HTTP). A local server runs with the user's authority and often with their environment, so installing one is installing code. A remote server needs authorization: the specification treats it as a resource server of an authorization framework based on OAuth, with protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728), resource indicators that bind a token to the server it is for (RFC 8707), proof key for code exchange, and the explicit rule that a server must not pass a token it received on to another service (token passthrough).
- Named problems in the specification's own security guidance: the confused deputy (a server acts for a client with authority the client did not grant), token passthrough, session hijacking, and local-server compromise. Added by the research community: tool poisoning (instructions hidden in a tool's description, which the model reads and the user does not), changes to a tool's definition after it was approved, a tool that shadows another's name, and results that carry instructions.
- Defences are the ones you know: audience-bound short-lived tokens, per-tool consent that shows the real arguments, pinning of tool definitions by hash with an alert on change, sandboxing of local servers with no ambient credentials, egress allow-lists, argument validation, logging.
- The specification is revised often. Pin the revision; read its change log; do not assume a rule you learnt is still in force.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write a small server with an official software development kit offering three tools (a note store, a URL fetcher, a file reader), and a client. Run it over standard streams first, then over HTTP behind your local authorization server.
2. Capture the messages and mark the actors, what each trusts and what each checks. Show the token's audience and what the server does with a token issued for another server.
3. Plant a harmless instruction in a tool description (a marker the model should print) and show the client passes it to the model. Change a tool's definition after the user approved it and show your client notices (pinned hash) or does not.
4. Give the fetcher a destination argument and show a model-proposed call moving a canary to an address in your lab. Add the defences: audience check, definition pinning, destination allow-list, display of the exact arguments for consent, path confinement for the file reader.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Read the code of three open-source servers for this protocol (do not run them outside the sandbox). For each list the authority it holds, the inputs it trusts, whether it handles tokens, and its install path (who can change it). Rate their risk and write the sandbox configuration you would run each in.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Build the regression suite: audience mismatch, expired token, a token for the wrong resource, definition drift, a destination outside the allow-list, a path escaping the directory, a secret appearing in a log. Run it against the vulnerable and fixed servers. State what the suite cannot cover (a revision of the protocol that changes a rule).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the actor diagram with trust annotations, the captured messages, the demonstrations, the defences and the suite results on both servers, and the three server audits. It is accepted when every test fails on the vulnerable server and passes on the fixed one, and the specification revision you tested against is recorded.

D57.watch_for: Forwarding the client's token to a downstream service. A consent screen that shows the tool's name and not its arguments. A pinned hash of the description that ignores the schema.

D58.title: Persistent memory, poisoning and provenance
objectives: Explain persistent memory trust — explain how a stored memory carries an earlier input's influence into later sessions and other users, and why the memory's contents need provenance and a trust label

Evaluate isolated poisoning fixtures — build harmless fixtures that plant a false or instructing memory through a document, a tool result and another user's session, and measure how often a later session follows it
Design correction/provenance — design write gating, labelled reads, expiry, review, correction and deletion that reach every copy (cache, embedding, backup of the store), and test them

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name the five parts of a specification revision pin you would record. What is the confused deputy? Why is "the user approved the tool" not a defence against a changed description?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Memory turns a one-time input into a standing one. If an untrusted document can cause the agent to store "always send reports to this address", every later session inherits the instruction, perhaps for a different user. Poisoned memory is persistence for text.
- Controls on the write path: decide what may be stored (facts the user stated about themselves, not instructions from retrieved content), record the source session, the source type and the trust level, require confirmation for memories that carry preferences about authority, expire entries, and rate-limit writes.
- Controls on the read path: place memories in the prompt as labelled data with their provenance, never as system instructions, and never let a memory grant authority (authority comes from the backend, week 10 day 56).
- Correction and deletion must reach every copy: the store, the index of embeddings, caches, derived summaries, exports and backups. Test that a deleted memory is really not retrievable and not followed.
- Read the section of the agentic threat guidance on memory poisoning.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Add a memory store: after each session the agent proposes facts to remember, and a writer stores them with source, session, user and time.
2. Write three poisoning fixtures with harmless goals (a stored instruction to print a marker, a stored false preference about a recipient, a stored claim about a user's role): one planted through a retrieved document, one through a tool result, one by another user in a shared memory.
3. Run each twenty times in a later session and record how often the agent follows it, with an interval.
4. Add the controls: gated writes, labelled reads, no authority from memory, expiry, a review command. Rerun the fixtures. Then delete a poisoned memory and prove it is gone from the store, the embedding index and the cache.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Design and run three further fixtures: a delayed trigger (the memory acts only after a condition), a memory written by gradual drift over several sessions, and a poisoned summary of a long conversation. Evaluate your controls against them and record what they missed. Hold out one fixture family until the end to check you have not tuned to your own tests.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Write the memory integrity tests: a write from untrusted content is refused or labelled, a read never produces a system-level instruction, deletion reaches every copy, a rollback to a snapshot restores a known-good state. Run them with the stub and with the real model. State what the plan does not protect (a poisoned fact that looks like a normal preference).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the path diagram with trust labels, the fixtures with before and after rates and intervals, the deletion proof, the rollback procedure and the test output. It is accepted when each poisoning fixture has a measured rate before and after and deletion is shown across every copy.

D58.watch_for: Letting the memory writer see the untrusted content as instructions. Deleting the row and leaving the embedding. Tuning controls to the fixtures you will report.

D59.title: A bounded red/blue experiment
objectives: Define bounded red/blue experiment — write, before running anything, a design with hypotheses, the attack set, the success metrics, the number of trials, the stopping rules, the controls to enable in each round and the bounds that contain the experiment
Observe behavior — run the rounds, capture the traces, and record attack success, task success and side effects with intervals and the model and settings used
Verify defensive controls — show with ablations that each control matters (remove it, the attack success rises) and that the controls do not destroy the task

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list three controls on the memory write path and two on the read path. What are the copies a deletion must reach? What made one of your fixtures delayed?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- An experiment answers a question you wrote down before you saw the data. Pre-registration means the hypotheses, the metrics, the sample sizes and the analysis are fixed first, so that you cannot look for a pattern after the fact. This program's own rules for single-learner experiments take the same view.
- Bounded means safe by construction: a sandbox, synthetic data, harmless goals, a budget, a kill switch, and a stated list of what will not be tried. The attacker may be a scripted set of inputs and, if you choose, an attacking agent inside the same bounds.
- Measure two things: attack success (the harmless goal reached) and task success (the legitimate task completed). A defence that stops every attack by stopping every task is not a defence. Report both with intervals.
- An ablation removes one control at a time to show what each contributes. A held-out attack family tests whether you tuned the defences to the attacks you knew.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write the design: two hypotheses (the structural controls remove the impact-bearing attacks; the statistical controls lower but do not remove the rest), the attack set of forty inputs in four families, the metrics, twenty trials per input, the controls for rounds A (none), B (statistical), C (structural), D (all), the bounds and the stop.
2. Freeze it in git with a timestamp before running.
3. Run the four rounds. Capture traces. Compute attack success and task success with intervals.
4. Run the ablations: from D remove one control at a time and record the change.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Run a held-out fourth family of attacks that you wrote but did not use while designing the controls, and an attacking agent with a bounded goal. Compare the result with the earlier rounds and state whether the defences generalised. Record every deviation from your pre-registered plan and why.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Turn the experiment into a repeatable check: one command that reruns the design, stores the results with model hash, settings and date, and compares them with the previous run using the intervals. Show it detects a weakened control. Write the one-page limits statement: what was not tried, where the sample is thin, what would change the conclusion.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the frozen design, the rounds' results with intervals, the ablations, the held-out result, the deviations list and the limits statement. It is accepted when the design predates the data in version control and every claim carries an interval and the settings.

D59.watch_for: Writing the hypotheses after seeing the table. A defence that wins by refusing the task. Omitting the runs that did not turn out as expected.

D61.title: AI assets, threats and test objectives
objectives: Identify AI assets/threats — list the assets of an AI system across its life cycle (data, labels, features, models, weights, indexes, prompts, tools, credentials, pipelines, logs, evaluation sets) and the classes of threat against each
Prioritize failure modes — rank the failure modes by impact and likelihood with evidence from your own systems and from public taxonomies, and justify the order
Define test objectives — turn the top failure modes into test objectives with a harmless goal, a measure, a sample size and a stop rule, tied to your pre-registered design method

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the elements of a pre-registered design. What did your held-out attack family test? Name two ways a memory can be deleted incompletely.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- An AI system has a life cycle: data is collected and labelled, a model is trained or chosen and packaged, a service is built around it, and people and other systems use its outputs. Each stage has assets and attackers. The national taxonomy of attacks on machine learning organises them for predictive systems (evasion at inference time, poisoning at training time, privacy attacks that extract data or infer membership) and for generative systems (misuse, direct and indirect prompt injection, supply chain attacks, and the security of agents).
- The public knowledge base of adversary behaviour against AI systems (ATLAS) extends the vocabulary of the enterprise knowledge base with tactics and techniques seen against machine learning systems; the enterprise knowledge base itself has added techniques for attacks on AI features. Use both for naming and coverage, as in week 5.
- Ranking needs evidence: what an attacker needs (access, knowledge, effort), what they gain, what you have observed in your own tests. A ranking with no evidence is an opinion; say which parts are opinion.
- A test objective names the failure mode, the harmless goal that demonstrates it, the measure, how many trials, and when to stop. Without a stop rule an experiment keeps going until it finds something.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Choose the system under study: your week 10 agent plus a small classifier you will train on day 62 (for example a spam filter over synthetic messages). List every asset at each life-cycle stage.
2. For each asset write the threats that apply using the taxonomy's classes, and the controls that exist today.
3. Rank the failure modes with a stated scale, citing the evidence: your week 9 and 10 results, public reports you have read, what an attacker would need.
4. Write eight test objectives for the top failure modes in the pre-registration format of day 59, each with a harmless goal, a measure, a sample size and a stop rule.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Threat-model a system you did not build: a public description of a retrieval assistant with fine-tuning and tools, for example a vendor's reference architecture. In ninety minutes produce its asset list, ten threats, a ranking and three test objectives, marking every statement you could not verify as an assumption.

sections.name: Defence and verification

Implement two. Remove a control and show the check fails. List the failure modes of your list that have no automated check and why.

sections.name: Evidence and report

It is accepted when each ranked threat cites evidence or says it is an opinion and each objective has a measure and a stop rule.

D62.title: Adversarial fixtures, observed output and uncertainty
objectives: Build controlled adversarial fixtures — build fixtures that probe a trained classifier (evasion by small input changes) and the agent (harmless-goal inputs), each with a stated goal, budget and stop rule

Evaluate observed output — grade the outputs with a written rubric, check the grading against labels you made by hand (and by yourself again a week later where you can), and say how reliable the grading is
Report uncertainty — report each result with the number of trials, an interval, the sensitivity to settings and the limits of the fixture set

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name the life-cycle stages and one asset of each. Which of your test objectives would you run first and why? What is a stop rule for?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Fixtures are the red team's reusable inputs, built to be harmless and repeatable. For a classifier, evasion means changing an input a little so that its output changes (words replaced, spacing, character swaps in a message) while a human reads it the same. For an agent the fixtures are the injection and memory cases of weeks 9 and 10.
- Grading generated output is a measurement problem. A rubric states what counts as success in words a second grader could apply. Another model can act as judge, but it is a model: measure its agreement with your hand labels, look for its biases (length, position, style) and never use it on the cases it was tuned on.
- Agreement is measured, not assumed: compare two graders (you and the judge, or you now and you later) with a chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa and read the disagreements.
- Uncertainty has several sources: the sampling of cases, the variation between runs, the sensitivity to prompt and settings, the reliability of the grader. Report the ones you measured and name the ones you did not.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Train a small spam classifier on a synthetic dataset. Write twenty evasion fixtures by editing messages with small changes a reader would ignore. Measure how often each changes the classifier's decision, over a set of messages with an interval.
2. Write the agent fixtures for three failure modes from yesterday's list (reveal a canary, call a tool with a marker, store a marker in memory). Run each twenty times.
3. Write the rubric for the agent fixtures. Grade eighty outputs by hand. Grade them with a judge model, and compute agreement and the disagreements.
4. Report each result with trials, interval, settings, and the grader's measured reliability.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Regrade forty of your outputs without looking at your earlier grades, and compute your agreement with yourself. Change the judge's prompt and the model's temperature and record how much each result moves. Decide which results are stable enough to report and which are not.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Add defences for the classifier (normalising inputs, ensembling or adversarial training on the fixtures) and for the agent (the controls of weeks 9 and 10). Rerun the fixtures on a held-out set you did not use to design the defences. Report what improved, what did not, and what a better-resourced attacker could still do.

sections.name: Evidence and report

It is accepted when every result has its trials, interval and settings, and the grader's reliability is reported.

D63.title: Model and dependency provenance
objectives: Trace model/dependency provenance — for each model, dataset, package and container image in the lab record where it came from, who published it, which version, which hash and under which licence

Assess licensing/integrity — check integrity (hashes, signatures, file format risks) and licence terms (including use restrictions of open-weight models) for each, and record what you could not verify

Define acquisition controls — define and implement controls for bringing new models and packages into the lab: allow-listed sources, hash pinning, scanning, quarantine, licence review and an approval record

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: write the interval method you use for rates and one case where it fails. Which of your fixtures is most sensitive to settings? State the rubric rule you were least sure of.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A model is code you did not write, in the form of data. Where it comes from, who made it, whether it is the file you think it is and what you may do with it are supply-chain questions. So are the packages it needs, the container it runs in and the datasets behind it.
- Formats matter: some checkpoint formats are executed when loaded (a serialised object format can run arbitrary code), others hold only tensors and cannot. Prefer formats that cannot execute code, scan the rest, and load unknown files only in a sandbox with no network and no credentials.
- Integrity: compare the hash with the publisher's, prefer signed artefacts (signature and identity of the signer), pin by hash and not by name or tag, and watch for lookalike names (a package or a model with a one-letter difference).
- Licence: open weights are not necessarily open source. Models, datasets and code each carry terms that may restrict use, field, scale or redistribution. Record the terms and who approved the use.
- Records: a bill of materials for software and a counterpart for machine learning components lists what the system is made of; provenance attestations say how an artefact was built.

D64.title: Data poisoning, privacy exposure and governance
objectives: Evaluate data poisoning — poison the training data of your small classifier in two ways (flipped labels, a trigger pattern) and measure the effect on accuracy and on triggered inputs, and test detection by data validation
Assess privacy exposure — show membership inference on an overfitted model, scan your corpus and logs for personal data, and list the places where data about a person persists
Define governance controls — specify and implement controls for data collection, provenance, access, retention and deletion, with checks that fail when a control is missing

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: what makes a checkpoint format dangerous to load? Why pin by hash and not by tag? Name three terms in a model licence that could restrict your use.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- Poisoning corrupts what a model learns. Availability attacks degrade it (flip labels at random); targeted attacks teach it a hidden behaviour (a trigger pattern that forces an output) while leaving ordinary accuracy almost unchanged, which is why accuracy alone does not detect them. Defences are provenance (know who wrote the data), validation (outliers, label consistency, duplicate and near-duplicate checks), and tests with candidate triggers. Retrieval corpora are poisoned the same way.
- Privacy: models can reveal facts about their training data. An overfitted model is more confident on examples it saw than on ones it did not, which lets an observer infer membership. Generative models can reproduce memorised strings. Prompts, logs, caches, embeddings and evaluation sets hold personal data too.
- Governance is the set of decisions you can show: what data you may collect and why, from whom, under which terms, how long you keep it, who can see it, how a person's data is found and deleted, how a dataset's licence is honoured. It needs checks, not only a document.
- This is engineering guidance, not legal advice: where a law or an agreement applies, ask the person who owns that question.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. On the synthetic classifier, flip a growing fraction of training labels and plot accuracy. Then add a trigger (a harmless token inserted into a few examples labelled as one class) and measure accuracy on clean data and the rate at which triggered inputs flip.
2. Write validation that would catch each: label-consistency checks, near-duplicate detection, a test that searches for tokens that flip decisions. Run it on the clean and poisoned sets.
3. Overfit a model on a small synthetic dataset and show a membership inference that uses the confidence gap, with its accuracy. Then regularise and show the gap shrink.
4. Scan your lab corpus, prompts and logs for personal data patterns (synthetic ones you planted) and list where each persists.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Write a data inventory for the whole lab: each dataset and store, its origin, licence, contents, who can access it, how long it is kept, how it is deleted, and whether personal data is present. Mark the rows you could not fill in. Choose the three riskiest rows and propose the control for each.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Implement three governance checks as code: every dataset has a licence and an owner, nothing older than its retention period remains, and a person's identifier can be found and removed across the corpus, index and logs. Plant a violation of each and show the check fails; show a deletion reaching the index and the logs. State what the checks do not know.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the poisoning curves and trigger results, the validation outcomes, the membership inference result before and after regularisation, the personal-data map, the inventory with unknowns marked, and the three checks. It is accepted when every poisoning claim has a measurement and every check has a planted violation that it catches.

D64.watch_for: Judging poisoning by accuracy alone. A deletion that leaves the embeddings. A governance document with no check behind it.

D65.title: Metrics, benchmark leakage and regression criteria
objectives: Define valid metrics — for a stated claim choose metrics that measure it, say what each does not measure, and fix scoring rules, sample sizes and the analysis before running
Detect benchmark leakage — test whether evaluation items appear in training, tuning or retrieval data (exact and near matches, canaries) and measure the effect on the score
Create regression criteria — define thresholds that use intervals, a held-out set that stays held out, and a gate that blocks a change when a measure worsens beyond its interval

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: name two checks that would catch a poisoned dataset and one thing neither can see. How does an overfitted model reveal membership? Where in the lab does personal data persist after a deletion?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A metric is valid for a claim if its value would change when the claim stops being true and would not change otherwise. Accuracy of a classifier says little about how often it is fooled; the share of fixtures that succeed says nothing about how often real traffic contains them. Write the claim first ("the assistant does not disclose documents the requester may not read"), then the measure, then what the measure cannot show.
- Leakage means evaluation data influenced the system under test: items present in a training or tuning set, in a retrieval corpus, in a system prompt's examples, or in the developer's memory. It inflates scores. Check by exact and near-duplicate search, by planting canary strings in held-out items, and by looking for impossible performance.
- Goodhart's law applies: a measure that becomes a target stops measuring. Keep a held-out set that you run rarely, rotate cases, and report the measures you did not optimise.
- A regression criterion compares a new result with a reference using intervals, so that noise does not block changes and real losses do.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write three claims for your application and classifier. For each choose a metric, a scoring rule, the sample size and the analysis, and write what the metric does not show.
2. Test for leakage: search your fine-tuning, retrieval and prompt example sets for exact and near matches of your evaluation items; plant canary strings in held-out items and see whether any appears in outputs or in the corpus.
3. Deliberately leak ten evaluation items into a training or retrieval set and measure how much the score rises. Record the inflation.
4. Write the regression criteria: thresholds on the interval, the rotation of the held-out set, and the stored reference results.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Take a public benchmark description and design a leakage test for it that you could run against a model or corpus you control. List what the test would show if it passed and if it failed, and what it could not show. Draft the paragraph of a report that states the limits honestly.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Implement the gate: a command that runs the evaluation, compares with the stored reference using intervals, checks that no held-out item appears in any corpus, and fails the change otherwise. Show it blocks a regression, a leaked item and an unrecorded change of settings. Record the cost in time and what it cannot guard (a metric that stopped meaning anything).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the claims and metrics with their limits, the leakage test results and the inflation measurement, the regression criteria and the gate's output on a clean change, a regression and a leak. It is accepted when each metric states what it does not measure and the gate is shown to block a leak.

D65.watch_for: A metric chosen because it is easy to compute. Held-out data used to pick between two designs. A score reported without the settings and the version.
