D66.title: Week 11 assessment (blind practical)
objectives: Assess unfamiliar AI scenario — build a threat model of an unseen AI system from its description and artefacts and run the bounded tests it allows
Produce evidence-linked findings — link every finding to an artefact, a test or a measurement, with uncertainty, and separate what you measured from what you assume
Verify control/limits — recommend and verify controls for the supply chain and data findings, and state the limits of every conclusion

sections.name: Blind practical
sections.markdown: Open the assessment in the application, start the attempt and read the task statement. Take the scenario from the source you fixed before the week and do not read its notes or its list of problems before the clock starts. Stop at 120 minutes.

sections.name: Remediation
sections.markdown: Grade yourself against the rubric before reading any answer key. For every criterion below your target find the cause in your method (the asset you did not list, the test with no stop rule, the licence you did not read) and repair it with a short exercise. Then redo the failed part on a different scenario.

sections.name: Report
sections.markdown: Write the report in the structure of the task statement: assets and threats, tests and results with uncertainty, supply-chain findings, data findings, controls, limits. Attach the evidence with SHA-256 values.

sections.name: Performance review
sections.markdown: Compare the grade with the week's targets: independent execution, every finding linked to evidence, results reported with uncertainty, supply chain and data covered, honest limits. Record the three habits that cost you most and one change for the capstone.

D66.watch_for: Running a test with no stop rule. A finding with no artefact behind it. Treating a signed artefact as a safe one.

D67.title: Capstone charter: scope, threat model and acceptance rules
objectives: Define scope and authorization — write the scope statement and rules of engagement for the estate: owner, systems and addresses in scope, permitted and forbidden actions, rate, window, data handling, escalation and stop condition, with the authorization of the owner recorded

Build integrated threat model — draw the estate as one system (zones, hosts, identities, applications, data stores, pipelines, AI components) and derive the threats that cross layers, ranked with reasons

Establish acceptance rules — define the severity rubric, the evidence standard, the coverage required of each layer, the reproducibility rule and the completion criteria of the assessment before starting it

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: write the scope statement you wrote on day 1 and name what you would now add. List the elements of a pre-registered design. What did your portfolio index for weeks 1 to 4 lack?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- An engagement starts with permission and limits, not with tools. The rules of engagement turn authorization into operating rules: what may be touched, how hard, when, with what data, who to call if something breaks, and what ends the work. The record of who authorized what, and when, is part of the evidence.
- A cross-layer threat model follows an attacker's route, not an organisation chart: from an exposed web feature to a service account, to a host, to a domain privilege, to data, and the same route for an assistant that holds credentials. Defensive findings are strongest where they cut a route at its cheapest point.
- Acceptance rules prevent two failures: stopping when you are tired and reporting only what was easy. Decide before the work how findings are rated (a severity rubric with stated criteria, for example a scoring system's base metrics adjusted by your environment's context), what counts as evidence for a finding, which layers must be covered and to what depth, and when the work is complete.
- Read the planning and reporting guidance of the national technical guide to security testing, and the severity scoring specification you will use.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Write the scope statement and rules of engagement for the estate and have the owner of the estate (you, as owner, in a separate signed note) authorize it. Include the stop condition and the escalation path for something unexpected.
2. Record the pre-assessment baseline: snapshots, hashes of configuration, the topology, the list of accounts, the telemetry sources, the model and tool list. This is what you will compare against when you verify fixes.
3. Draw the estate as one data-flow diagram with trust boundaries and mark the five routes of greatest concern from outside to the canary.
4. Write the acceptance rules: severity rubric, evidence standard, coverage per layer, the reproducibility rule (each finding reproduced twice, by a second method where possible) and the completion criteria.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Without opening the sealed list, write an assessment plan for the estate: the order of work, the time box for each layer, what you will do if a layer is larger than expected, and which of the five routes you will test first and why. Then review your plan against the rules of engagement and strike anything that is out of scope.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Verify the baseline is usable: from the recorded baseline, restore the estate in a clean copy and show that the baseline's hashes match and the topology is identical. Write the check that detects drift from the baseline and run it after a deliberate small change. State what the baseline does not cover (state that lives only in memory).

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the scope statement and authorization note, the baseline with hashes and restore proof, the integrated diagram with the five routes, the acceptance rules and the assessment plan. It is accepted when a stranger could tell from the charter what may be tested, how a finding is rated and when the work is done.

D67.watch_for: A scope written after the first scan. Acceptance rules written after seeing what is easy. A baseline taken after the assessment started.

D68.title: Network and application assessment
objectives: Assess isolated network — map the estate's zones and test its segmentation and name resolution against its intended policy within scope, interpreting discovery results with confidence

Evaluate controlled app weaknesses — test the web application and API for access control, token, request-forgery, upload and logic weaknesses, with two tenants and several roles, and prove each finding safely
Document remediation — for each finding write the root cause, the smallest remediation and a regression test, and apply and verify the ones within your remit

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the five routes of your charter and the layer each starts in. What was the stop condition you wrote? Which acceptance rule would stop you from reporting only easy findings?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- An assessment works through layers against a policy: what the network is meant to allow, what the application is meant to do for whom. Findings are differences between intent and reality, each with a cause, an effect and a cost to fix.
- Chain findings with care: a low-severity weakness that completes a route to the canary may matter more than a medium one that leads nowhere. Rate each finding alone and its place in a chain.
- Reproduce every finding twice and by a second method where you can, using synthetic data and harmless markers. A finding that cannot be reproduced is a lead, not a finding; say so.
- Remediation is part of the job: the smallest change that removes the cause, with a test that failed before and passes after.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Within the scope, map the zones and compare the observed flows with the intended policy using the matrix of week 2. Interpret discovery results with confidence labels and note every difference.
2. Test name resolution and the router's rules for the differences that matter to your routes.
3. Test the web application and API as two tenants and the roles of week 4, following the checklist of classes: access control, tokens, request forgery, uploads and import, business logic, injection and output encoding.
4. For each finding record the evidence, a second reproduction, the severity under your rubric, and the route it belongs to.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Take the layer or class you tested least thoroughly in the guided block and test it again with a different method (a different tool, or by reading code and configuration instead of probing). Compare the findings and record what the second method added.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Fix what is in your remit: apply the smallest remediation for each finding, write the regression test, and show that the test fails on the baseline and passes after. Re-run the segmentation matrix and the access-control matrix and update the drift check. State which findings you could not fix and why.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the findings table (evidence, second reproduction, severity, route, root cause, remediation, test), the matrices before and after, and the list of unfixed findings. It is accepted when every finding was reproduced twice and every fixed finding has a test that fails on the baseline.

D68.watch_for: Testing as one tenant. A finding reported from a single run. Fixing the symptom and not the cause.
D68.resources:
- `https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/`: Web Security Testing Guide, stable release to be confirmed when you read it. OWASP project, open licence stated by the project, ASSUMED
- `https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x00-header/`: OWASP API Security Top 10, 2023 edition. OWASP project, open licence stated by the project, ASSUMED

D69.title: Host and identity assessment
objectives: Assess host/identity boundaries — enumerate the Linux and Windows hosts and the domain as a low-privilege principal and find the privilege paths and the trust problems
Explain access chain — explain the chain from the application foothold of the previous day to host and domain privilege as one path, with the right, trust or misconfiguration behind each step
Verify controls — cut the chain at its cheapest points, re-enumerate to show the chain is gone, and confirm the hardening baseline holds on every host in the chain

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the severity criteria of your rubric. Which of your findings yesterday belongs to more than one route? How would you show a stranger that a fix works?

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- A chain is a sequence of steps each of which gives the next its starting point: an application account that can read a configuration file, a credential in it that is valid on a host, a service on that host that runs with a privilege, a delegation or a write right in the directory. The weakest link is not the most severe finding but the one whose removal cuts the most chains.
- Explain every step in terms of a boundary: whose authority, which check, why it did not hold. A step that you cannot explain is one you have not understood and cannot fix with confidence.
- Cutting a chain means choosing the cheapest effective edge, and verifying means collecting again. A verification that reuses the original step's method proves the step is closed; a different method proves the chain is.
- Hardening verification is behavioural, as in week 5.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Enumerate the Linux hosts, the Windows hosts and the domain as a low-privilege principal: sudo and capabilities, writable privileged files, services and their paths, persistence, delegation, rights on privileged objects, tokens and groups.
2. Join the application foothold of day 68 to what you find: which credential, which host, which service, which right. Draw the chain and mark the boundary at each step.
3. Reproduce the chain twice with harmless markers. State for every step why it works.
4. Rate the chain and each step under your rubric.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Search for a second chain that does not use the first foothold (a different entry point or a different privilege route). If you find one, document it; if not, document what you tried and what coverage you had, so that the null result can be read.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Cut each chain at its cheapest edge and re-enumerate with a different method from the one that found it. Run the behavioural hardening tests of week 5 on the hosts in the chain and the identity checks of week 6 on the domain. Update the drift check. Record what remains and why.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the enumeration records, the chain diagram with the boundary for each step, the reproductions, the cuts with the re-enumeration, and the hardening test output. It is accepted when every step of every chain is explained as a boundary and the chains are shown gone by a different method.

D69.watch_for: Reporting a tool's path without the right behind each edge. Verifying a fix with the same step that found the flaw. Ignoring the hosts that are not on the first chain.
D69.resources:

D70.title: Detection, investigation and response reasoning
objectives: Build telemetry/detection — build detections for the steps of the chains you found, with fixtures, conversions and a false-positive estimate against the estate's baseline
Investigate incident scenario — investigate the benign incident planted in the estate's telemetry from a stated hypothesis, correlating host, network and identity evidence into a labelled timeline
Demonstrate IR reasoning — scope and rate the incident, choose and justify containment, eradication and recovery steps with their risks, and state what you could not determine

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the steps of your chain on the host side and the telemetry each would leave. What is the difference between observed and inferred? Write one sentence for each of containment, eradication and recovery.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- The detections of the capstone follow the chains: a detection is valuable where it sits on several chains, early, and with a cost you can bear. Write the hypothesis, the rule, the fixtures and the estimate as in week 7; ask of each how an adversary could avoid it and what it would take.
- An investigation needs a hypothesis before the search, a record of queries and joins, and a timeline whose statements are labelled. Incident response reasoning then asks what is affected, how bad, what to do first, and what each action risks, including what it destroys.
- A recommendation is a decision aid: who decides, what the options are, what each costs and risks, what evidence supports it, what is still unknown, and when to review.
- Combine the evidence kinds: a name lookup, a connection, a process start and a logon become one story only when joined on identifiers you can name.

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. For the steps of your chains write six detections with hypotheses, positive and negative fixtures, a conversion check and an estimate of false positives per day over the estate's baseline. Choose where each runs.
2. State a hypothesis for the planted incident before you search. Investigate it across host, network and identity telemetry with a record of queries.
3. Build the timeline with every statement labelled observed, inferred or assumed.
4. Write the scoping and severity decision, with criteria, and the containment, eradication and recovery recommendation with risks.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Hunt in the same telemetry for something your detections did not target, using a hypothesis drawn at random from the techniques list. Record the coverage and the result, including a null result. Then compare what your detections would have caught of the planted incident with what the investigation found by hand, and list the gap.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Run the detections against replays of your own chain reproductions and against the baseline: they must fire on the first and stay within budget on the second. Measure time from the chain's step to the alert. Record the evasions you know and a plan to close the cheapest. Rehearse the incident decision in ten minutes as if speaking to the owner of the estate and note what you could not say with evidence.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the detections with fixtures and estimates, the replay results, the investigation record and labelled timeline, the response recommendation with its risks, and the evasion list. It is accepted when each detection has negative fixtures and a measured rate, each timeline statement is labelled, and each recommendation states its risk.

D70.watch_for: Rules with no negative fixture. A timeline that mixes inference into observation. A containment recommendation that destroys the evidence.

- `https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/61/r3/final`: SP 800-61, the current revision; note which revision you read. NIST publication, freely available, ASSUMED

D71.title: AI and agent assessment
objectives: Assess an AI/agent workflow — map the assistant's retrieval, the agent's loop, tools and the MCP server, with identities and authority crossings, and connect them to the chains of the estate

Test authorized trust boundaries — test, with harmless goals, the retrieval permissions, the tools' authority, the token handling of the MCP server and the injection paths, within the authorization of the charter

Verify mitigations — apply and verify the structural mitigations (typed enforcement, delegated authority, memory write controls) with deterministic tests and a pre-registered measurement for the model-dependent ones

sections.name: Recall
sections.markdown: Without notes: list the three questions to ask of every tool. What does a scripted adversarial model prove? State the chain-of-evidence rule for a model-dependent finding.

sections.name: Theory
sections.markdown:
- In an estate the AI components are not a separate subject: the assistant holds credentials, reads documents and calls tools that reach the same hosts and domain as the rest. A finding in the assistant is a route into the estate or from it, and belongs in the same threat model and rating as any other.
- The tests are those of weeks 9 and 10, applied to the estate's components: retrieval permissions checked in code, tool authority derived from the requester, tokens bound to their audience, tool definitions pinned, memory writes gated, limits enforced outside the model.
- Separate what the application guarantees (tested with a stub, expected to pass) from what the model does (measured, reported with intervals, with the model version and settings).

sections.name: Guided lab
sections.markdown:
1. Map the assistant, agent and MCP server of the estate with the identity and authority at each crossing, and connect each crossing to a route in the integrated diagram.
2. Test the boundaries with harmless fixtures: a canary in a restricted document, a tool call carrying a marker, a token for another server, a changed tool description, a stored instruction in memory.
3. Record each finding with its reproduction and the boundary it crosses; run the model-dependent ones twenty times and report intervals.
4. Rate each finding in the estate's context: what it gives an attacker on the chains.

sections.name: Independent lab
sections.markdown: Write a pre-registered mini experiment for the one model-dependent control that matters most to the estate, run it, and report the result with the design date shown in version control. Add the attacking input family you held out.

sections.name: Defence and verification
sections.markdown: Apply the structural fixes and verify them: stub tests for retrieval, authority, tokens, definition pinning and memory, and the measured rates before and after for the model-dependent control. Update the estate's drift check to include the AI components. State what remains and the owner who must decide on it.

sections.name: Evidence and report
sections.markdown: Hand in the map with crossings, the findings with boundaries, the stub tests, the measured rates with intervals and settings, the pre-registered design and the fixes. It is accepted when every guarantee has a stub test and every statistic has an interval and a settings record.

D71.watch_for: Treating the assistant as outside the estate's threat model. A model-dependent finding reported without a rate. Fixing the prompt and calling it a control.

D72.title: Capstone: blind integrated practical, defence of findings and portfolio
objectives: Complete blind integrated practical — assess an unfamiliar estate across layers within the time box, following an access chain to the canary and recommending controls and detections
Defend findings with evidence — for each claim present the evidence, the reproduction, the alternatives excluded and the limits, and answer questions on it as in a review with the owner of the estate
Deliver final CT9 portfolio — assemble the portfolio of all twelve weeks with an index, hashes and a self-assessment, and record what you can do, what you cannot yet, and what you will study next

sections.name: Blind practical
sections.markdown: Open the assessment in the application, start the attempt and read the task statement. Take the estate from the source you fixed before the week and do not read its notes or its list of faults before the clock starts. Stop at 120 minutes.

sections.name: Remediation
sections.markdown: Grade yourself against the rubric before reading any answer key. For every criterion below your target find the cause in your method across the twelve weeks (the habit that first appeared in week 1 or 3 and still costs you) and repair it with a targeted exercise from the week that taught it. Redo the part of the practical that failed on a fresh copy of the estate where you can.

sections.name: Report
sections.markdown: Write the capstone report: an executive summary for the owner (what is wrong, what matters most, what to do first, what you could not determine) and a technical part (scope, method, findings with severity, evidence and reproduction, chains, detections, response reasoning, remediation and verification, limits). Then defend it: record yourself answering the ten hardest questions a reviewer could ask, and state the evidence for each answer.

sections.name: Performance review
sections.markdown: Assemble the portfolio: an index of the twelve weeks' hand-ins with hashes, the capstone report, a self-assessment for each of the 64 competencies (what evidence supports it, what is missing), the gap list ranked by consequence, and a plan for the next twelve weeks. Then review the program: which habits changed, which did not, which week taught the most, and what you would change in this curriculum.

D72.watch_for: Leaving the scope check until later. Reporting breadth with no chain. Writing the executive summary last, in a hurry, and for yourself.
